Did The First Quarks and Gluons Experience Brownian Motion? Sometimes.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe.
  • Recent findings suggest that the fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos.
  • Industry observers note that particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe. One is to peer into the deepest, darkest regions of space. The other is to study the most dense energetic fluid we can create in particle accelerators. A newly introduced study looks at how this fluid can behave.

Recent findings suggest that the fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos. In those earliest moments quarks churned among the sea of strong-force carrier particles, similar to the way dust particles dance in a swirl of atomosphere molecules. Only after the Universe expanded a bit did this fluid solidify into the nuclei we see today. By slamming particles together at near light speeds, we can recreate a bit of that early plasma fluid, but only for the briefest moments of time. So we study the fluid primarily by the particles generated by these collisions. In this fresh study the team simulated how the fluid behaves when a heavy particle passes through it. In the lab this can be done by slamming a proton into a heavy nucleus.

Industry observers note that particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion. First observed by Robert Brown as the jiggly motion of pollen in water, it occurs when smaller particles collide with a larger particle over time. The barrage of kicks nudges the larger particle around a jiggly random path. The smaller particles also collide with each other in a similar way. On a large scale this creates many of the features of thermodynamics, such as the flow of heat and the ideal gas relation of temperature and pressure.

According to recent reports, one of the features of Brownian motion is that the distribution of particle speeds is Gaussian. Most of the particles have speeds close to the average, but there are some particles that are much faster and some that are much slower. The distribution is symmetrical; for every 10 particles moving twice as fast as the average, there should be about 10 moving half as fast. This makes sense because collisions are random.

How the Gaussian particle distribution is shifted for higher-energy collisions. Credit: Du Plessis et al.

Recent findings suggest that although a dense plasma of charged gluons is very different from a drop of water molecules, they both follow this Gaussian distribution. After all, they are both a sea of randomly colliding molecules. You would expect then that when heavy particles move through the plasma, the result would be Gaussian. All the heavy particles would be slowed down passing through the plasma, but some would slow a bit more and others a bit less because of the random collisions. This fresh study found that for heavy quarks in a quark-gluon plasma this is only partially true.

Sources indicate that at slower speeds the result is precisely what we would expect. Collisions are random, and heavy quarks would have a Gaussian speed distribution. But if the heavy quarks are moving at near-light speed, such as a proton in a particle collider, then the distribution is biased. The quark is much more likely to be kicked in a way that slows it down and much less likely to get a kick that speeds it up. This skews the distribution away from Gaussian.

This means that when we study quark-gluon plasmas in a particle accelerator, we must take this bias into account. Using this result, we can better understand the fluid as a whole, and this could help us understand the connection between the hot dense state of the Significant Bang and the Universe we see today.

Du Plessis, Jean F., and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld. "Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm." Physical Review Letters 137.19 (2026): 192302. ↩.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clay figurines from the Middle East suggest that artistic traditions were already being shared across generations before farming, possibly with children taking part in their creation.

It has been revealed that long before agriculture transformed life in the Middle East, people were already shaping clay into figures that reflected the world around them. Some resembled birds, mammals, and humans, while others carried traces of red or orange coloring. One fragment may even depict the facial markings of a mountain gazelle.

It has been revealed that these small artifacts, originally excavated from three sites in present-day Israel, date back roughly 15,000 to 11,500 years. Researchers believe they provide the earliest known evidence of a clay figurine-making tradition in the region, suggesting that people were using the material for symbolic expression much earlier than previously thought.

It has been revealed that at the time, the region was home to Natufian communities, hunter-gatherers who had begun living in permanent settlements before the development of agriculture. Archaeologists already knew that Natufian people made figurines, although most previously discovered examples were fashioned from bone or stone.

In a recent development, clay figurines, by contrast, were generally believed to have become common during the Neolithic period, when the agricultural revolution began around 11,500 years ago. The newly identified objects suggest that the practice had much deeper roots, revealing a wider range of artistic expression among these early communities.

The findings also raise questions about how cultural traditions developed before farming. The researchers suggest that Natufian artistic practices were more varied and complex than previously recognized, and that some aspects of the region’s later Neolithic culture may have originated thousands of years earlier.

According to recent reports, the research, published November 11, 2026, in the open-access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Dr. Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel and colleagues. Beyond revealing an earlier history of clay figurines, the study offers clues about how creative practices and cultural knowledge may have passed between generations.

“These discoveries change how we understand the beginnings of artistic expression in the first villages of humanity. Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world. What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations,” stated Davin.

Reference: “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia” by Laurent Davin, Marion Sindel, Mina Weinstein-Evron, Reuven Yeshurun, Daniel Kaufman, Leore Grosman, Anna Belfer-Cohen, Hamoudi Khalaily and François R. Valla, 11 November 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360388.

Tiny Grains of Sand Could Reveal What the Weather Was Like on Mars Billions of Years Ago

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered a surprising connection between sand grain size and the winds that shape dunes on Earth and Mars.
  • According to recent reports, the size of a sand grain could reveal how fast the wind was blowing when a desert dune formed, even billions of years ago.
  • Windblown dunes and ripples have been identified on Venus, Mars, Saturn’s moon Titan, and even a comet orbiting the sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered a surprising connection between sand grain size and the winds that shape dunes on Earth and Mars.

According to recent reports, the size of a sand grain could reveal how fast the wind was blowing when a desert dune formed, even billions of years ago. Stanford University researchers have discovered that dunes on Earth and Mars are primarily shaped by winds traveling just above the minimum speed needed to move sand. Their findings offer a way to reconstruct ancient winds using sediment preserved in planetary landscapes.

Windblown dunes and ripples have been identified on Venus, Mars, Saturn’s moon Titan, and even a comet orbiting the sun. Their shapes and patterns provide evidence of prevailing wind directions and how consistently winds have blown, but determining wind speeds has been much more difficult.

According to recent reports, in a study published November 16 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers demonstrated that the wind speeds responsible for most dune formation are closely linked to the median size of the sand grains. Stronger winds can transport larger particles, while finer grains generally require less force to move.

The relationship depends on a critical threshold: the wind must be strong enough to set sand grains in motion along the ground. Although faster winds can transport more sediment, the researchers found that winds only modestly exceeding this threshold account for much of the sand movement that builds dunes.

The research builds on a hypothesis proposed by University of Pennsylvania scientists in 2010, suggesting that dunes develop mainly under winds slightly stronger than those needed to initiate sand transport. “Since then, nobody’s really looked at this idea, even though it’s really powerful because it tells you something about the environmental conditions that formed the dune fields that we see on not just Earth and Mars, but on a variety of other planetary bodies,” mentioned lead author Colin Marvin, who conducted the research as a PhD student at Stanford.

In a recent development, to test the idea, the team examined 30 years of wind observations alongside sand grain measurements from 24 dune fields worldwide. The sites encompassed different dune shapes, sizes, and environments, including Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah and the ancient desert landscapes of Namibia.

It has been revealed that for each location, the researchers calculated which wind speed transported the greatest amount of sand over time. Across all 24 fields, that speed was closely associated with grain size and remained only slightly above the threshold required to move the sediment.

The team next examined measurements from a Martian dune field, where the relationship between sand size and the winds responsible for dune formation was similar to that observed on Earth. This held despite major differences in atmospheric pressure, gravity, and sediment density between the two planets.

It has been revealed that the results suggest that the same basic process may govern dune formation on other worlds, provided loose sediment is abundant and stronger winds become progressively less frequent. Marvin described dunes as a “great recorder of what happens on a planet’s surface, and particularly the interactions between what’s happening in the atmosphere of a planet and what’s happening on the surface.”.

Because sand grains can survive long after the winds that transported them have disappeared, the relationship could help scientists estimate ancient wind speeds from sedimentary rocks. It may also provide a way to test models of atmospheric circulation during periods when Earth’s atmosphere differed substantially from its present state.

The discovery could help researchers “better reconstruct winds and climates through time, on Earth and beyond,” noted senior author Mathieu Lapôtre, associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. “It works for modern dunes and for sandstones dating back three billion years.”.

Such reconstructions could be used to investigate the atmospheric histories of both Earth and Mars. According to Lapôtre, the research is already moving in that direction. “Colin is actively working on that, actually. He’s already pushing on to the next steps.”.

The study was supported by a National Science Foundation CAREER grant.

“If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed ... and we will deserve it.”.

Reflecting on Tuesday’s midterm election results, a shellacking by Democrats that served as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, this quote deserves another look.

Recent findings suggest that in 2016, in the midst of a heated Republican primary race, with assorted candidates jockeying to be the party’s presidential nominee, those words were posted by what now seems a surprising source: South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Of course, Graham himself had been one of the candidates in that bitter contest. Insults like “lightweight” and “jackass” were tossed back and forth, and Trump publicly shared Graham’s cellphone number. (Trump finally apologized for that stunt — at Graham’s funeral this past July. Better late than never, I suppose.).

By the time of Graham’s death this year, though, his earlier self would not have recognized the senator from South Carolina who had transformed himself into one of the president’s golfing buddies and closest allies.

In May of this year, after Sen. Bill Cassidy lost his Louisiana primary to a Trump-backed opponent, Graham reasoned on NBC News that Cassidy lost because he “tried to destroy” the president, and warned the same fate would befall any Republican who crossed Trump. “This is the party of Donald Trump.”.

Why the switch? “He allowed me into his world. That’s great,” he told The Latest York Times.

Lindsey Graham stayed relevant, with a desired seat at the table — at a cost to his political reputation and legacy.

It has been revealed that after he died, Graham’s sister was appointed to complete his Senate term and was then pushed to run for a full term by her brother’s onetime nemesis Donald Trump. The president’s endorsement pushed Darline Graham past a more experienced Republican, Rep. Ralph Norman, in the Senate primary.

That she played a part in the Republicans’ historic midterm loss is a full-circle moment that Shakespeare would relish.

Recent findings suggest that graham lost to Dr. Annie Andrews, as the state elected a Democratic senator for the first time in decades. It came as a significant surprise, especially to those Republicans who, like Lindsey Graham, started out as skeptics of the inexperienced, cruel president before making peace with the man, his policies and his power.

MAGA swallowed the GOP, and voters who elected Trump in 2016 and 2024 followed.

What was the breaking point for the people who ignored millions of dollars in attack ads on their way to the polls?

In Ohio, was it the Vivek Ramaswamy ad that dredged up opponent Amy Acton’s childhood trauma, supported by Trump and Vice President JD Vance?

In the South, was it the seeming glee of Republican state legislatures as they gerrymandered districts with substantial African American constituencies, all with the blessing of a Supreme Court-weakened Voting Rights Act?

In Texas, did Hispanic voters who swung to Trump in 2024 realize that ICE’s definition of “the worst of the worst” included business owners, grandmoms and schoolchildren?

Did tariffs turn off farmers as it affected expenses and bottom lines?

Did Americans rebel when they saw their dollars buy less while the president gushed over gold trinkets, a ballroom and a reflecting pool his hand-picked contractors couldn’t fix, and made billions for himself and his family?

Did the Islamophobia and anti-Semitism, the racism and homophobia in the name of Jesus leave true people of faith or just plain decent people disgusted?

In South Carolina, Darline Graham didn’t explain her aims for the economy or for fighting corruption or foreign entanglements, except to say “national security is not my thing” on a debate stage.

But the candidate with a scant resume did manage at a South Carolina rally to call her opponent “bats — crazy” while standing next to an approving Trump, who coined his own anti-trans slur for Andrews.

Andrews responded by saying: “If name-calling would help lower gas prices and grocery prices, he can call me all the names he wants. But I don’t think that’s going to get the job done.” In a state with 14 counties “without a single OB/Gyn,” as Andrews has noted, the emptiness of insults is hard to miss.

Whatever lessons they draw from Tuesday, Democrats should not get comfortable.

Angry, hurting voters expect results — fast.

But for now, it’s hard not to recall the warning issued and then forgotten 10 years ago, with the hope that Republicans realize the old Lindsey might have been right all along.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, there’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast.
  • Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

According to recent reports, there’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Sources indicate that making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a significant party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

Sources indicate that dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with significant flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

Recent findings suggest that the recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Searching for Elusive Signals in the Cosmic Microwave Background from the South Pole

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the oldest observable light in the cosmos, the Cosmic Microwave Background is a fundamental signal that has a lot to teach us about the Universe.
  • But the CMB has also changed over time with the expansion of the Universe.
  • According to recent reports, two space telescopes have played crucial roles in mapping the CMB: the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probee (WMAP), and the Planck satellite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the oldest observable light in the cosmos, the Cosmic Microwave Background is a fundamental signal that has a lot to teach us about the Universe. It dates back to the recombination epoch, when photons could first travel freely through the cosmos. The CMB is like a snapshot of the state of energy and matter about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

But the CMB has also changed over time with the expansion of the Universe. As the Universe has expanded, the CMB has been stretched into microwave wavelengths that we can't see. That's why, despite containing the overwhelming majority of the Universe's photons, we can't see it without the help of telescopes.

According to recent reports, two space telescopes have played crucial roles in mapping the CMB: the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probee (WMAP), and the Planck satellite. They were both up above the obscuring effect of Earth's atmosphere, which is the main obstacle to observing the CMB. The CMB is nearly uniform, but not quite. It has tiny irregularities that cosmologist have mapped in increasing detail. These small temperature inhomogeneities can reveal a lot about the Universe and the Big Bang.

According to recent reports, this is the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe's heat map of temperature fluctuations in the Cosmic Microwave Background. (Credit : NASA / WMAP Science Team).

But there's also another way of studying the CMB. The South Pole Telescope is a 10-meter radio telescope in Antarctica that takes advantage of a small atmospheric window to observe part of the CMB. It's also in a designated "radio-quiet zone." It's credited with discovering a fresh feature of the CMB called the B-mode polarization. Gravitational lensing by intervening matter like galaxy clusters created this B-mode polarization. That proved that the CMB can hold evidence of gravitatonal effects.

In a recent development, that was a major deal because the polarization had been predicted decades earlier. The CMB's polarization is almost perfectly uniform. But almost isn't completely, and there are tiny variations in the B-mode polarity. In this case, these tiny changes were created by intervening matter.

In a recent development, the CMB's polarization was first detected in 2002, and that was a massive accomplishment. John Carlstrom from the University of Chicago led the collaboration that detected it, and he is now the director of the South Pole Telescope. âWe were sitting around with a small team, looking at our computer. There were peaks and wiggles, just as predicted,â Carlstrom noted. âWe were just staring at it and it was just phenomenal.â.

According to recent reports, the South Pole Telescope hard at work during the long polar night. Image Credit: Report of the U.S. Antarctic Program Blue Ribbon Panel - More and Better Science in Antarctica Through Increased Logistical Effectiveness, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/25790806.

âItâs one of the ways that we can understand gravity at these very extreme scales,â mentioned Kimmy Wu, an assistant professor at the California Institute of Technology, one of the institutions involved in the south pole observations. âThe fact that there could be primordial gravitational waves means that at the early fraction of a second when the universe was quantum fluctuations, gravity worked.â.

According to recent reports, quantum gravity can only be detected in this very early fraction of a second. It's beyond the capabilities of supercolliders to examine, and these tiny waves are the only way to observe quantum gravity. If quantum gravity can be detected in the very first moments of the Universe, then it can help physicists bridge the gap between General Relativity, which describes things on a massive scale, and quantum physics, which describes things on a tiny scale. So finding these tiny primordial gravitational waves brings us closer to a unified theory of how everything works. That would be nice; just ask any physicist.

This graphic helps explain the complicated problem facing physicists. If they can detect B-mode polarization in the CMB, it's evidence that quantum fluctuations generated primordial gravitational waves. Image Credit: By Original: DrbogdanâVector: Yinweichen - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/31825049.

But as stated earlier, these first B-mode detections were due to gravitational lensing, not quantum gravity. The next natural question was, can the B-mode contain evidence of primordial, quantum gravity? A latest instrument was needed to find out.

Next to the South Pole Telescope is the Background Imaging of Cosmic Extragalactic Polarization (BICEP) array. BICEP was built to measure the B-mode polarization of the CMB that come directly from quantum gravity. The current iteration of BICEP is the fifth, and overall, it's been working since 2006.

If BICEP can detect these tiny gravitational ripples from the Universe's very beginnings, then our understanding of the tiniest workings of the Universe will take shape. It would provide the most robust evidence for inflation and Substantial Bang cosmology.

Members of the BICEP team in front of BICEP. The array is articulated and sits inside a specially designed protective blue windproof and thermally insulated cover. Image Credit: BICEP Array.

âIf we could detect these B-modes robustly, then itâs bulletproof,â said Lindsey Bleem, a physicist at DOEâs Argonne National Laboratory who worked at the South Pole in 2008 and 2014.

If they can rule out these B-modes, then physicists need to revise models of inflation or work on other ones. Either way, it's progress.

But there's another mode of CMB polarization called E-mode. They are both weaker and harder to detect than temperature fluctuations in the CMB. In fact, the E-mode is only one-tenth as strong as the temperature fluctuations, and the B-mode is even weaker.

Recent findings suggest that âWe are here in the business of making a super, super precise measurement. This is basically a few nanokelvin on top of the 2.725 [degrees] of the CMB,â noted Zeeshan Ahmed, associate professor at Stanford University and researcher at DOEâs SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory.

This image indicates an illustration of the Planck satellite over the satellite's map of the CMB. It's work was an improvement of the WMAP's map. Image Credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration - D. Ducros.

Sources indicate that when measuring something so faint, interference becomes a major problem. Other radiation sources can pollute signals, the Milky Way's dust can add its own polarization, and some E-modes can transform into B-modes. It all adds up to one of the most complicated challenges in science.

But the SPT and BICEP each have different strengths, and by working together, scientists think they can find a way forward. âItâs like a marriage,â said Bleem. âBICEP has the intense sensitivity at large scales and SPT can make these wonderful gravitational lensing maps, without which BICEP would be completely limited by the systematics. Together, they can achieve the targeted goals.â.

Other telescopes like Herschel and Planck contribute too, by sorting out and mapping sources of interference in the signal that can lense the E-mode signal.

It has been revealed that âIf there is a signal, you should be able to see that in both places,â said Wu. âThese are excellent ways to really check whether a claim of detection is substantiated.â.

According to recent reports, that was an important step. It provided a way to determine what E-modes had been warped by gravity to appear like B-modes. That was a potential way through the mess.

âBeing able to measure that signal for the first time â¦ was very exciting,â recalled Carlstrom.

In 2014, the BICEP2 team presented a paper to their peers showing that they had detected B-mode polarization indicating a gravitational wave signal from inflation. Their excitement was short-lived though. Subsequent examination and fresh data from other researchers indicated that the signal could be attributed to the Milky Way's problematic dust.

This image illustrates how the Milky Way's dust can polarize the CMB. Image Credit: ESA.

Industry observers note that âWe dialed up our skepticism on these things in the last ten years,â remarked Ahmed, who works on the BICEP Array. âIf latest data is coming in and it can be co-analyzed with ours, we would love that.â.

In a recent development, work continues on this complicated problem, and the potential payoff is so monumental that setbacks aren't deterring the researchers. They continue to work on eliminating sources of uncertainty in the data.

According to recent reports, they're getting a better handle on how gravitational lensing affects data and how to understand what mode of polarization they're sensing. They're improving instrument precision and eliminating more noise. Upcoming improvements to both the South Pole Telescope and BICEP will drive further progress.

Recent findings suggest that for now, there's no unambiguous detection of primordial gravitational waves. But work continues in the extreme conditions at the bottom of the world, with ever-improving telescopes and the apparent unbreakable will of the dedicated researchers.

âIt is really rewarding to see the SPT. When I started working on it, it was just a proposal â we hadnât built the telescope yet,â said Benson. âThe fact that we can still do cutting-edge science with it and sustaining it over 20 years has been really satisfying.â.

9 Best Coffee Subscriptions, Reviewed & Reordered (2026)

📅 23 Sep 2021 | ⏱️ 35 min read (7067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~35 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans.
  • Whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a latest craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you.
  • I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans. That’s where coffee subscriptions come in. But the best services will do more than guarantee you’ll have a consistent supply of freshly roasted coffee—they also let you explore the vast world of coffee. They’re how I’ve discovered some of my favorite roasters, tried single-origins I never would have found on my own, and figured out exactly what I like and don’t like in a cup.

Whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a latest craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you. After five years of testing, Trade is our top pick—but depending on what kind of coffee you like, I have plenty of other recommendations.

I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers. To date, we’ve tested nearly two dozen options and recommend the following wholeheartedly.

Fresh in this enhancement: BA editors have been trying out some new deliveries, including some we’re loving from Methodical in Greenville, SC, and Fellow’s Drops program.

Trade is a multi-roaster subscription that sources coffee from independent roasters all over the country. It's great for someone looking for great specialty coffee with an interest in trying a number of different roasters and different roasting styles.

Recent findings suggest that tester: Chris Morocco, food director This was the easiest subscription I have ever set up, and Trade did such a good job of hitting my preferences right in their sweet spot: medium roast, medium body, medium fruit…just medium all around. I have gotten stuck in the past, tasting the same coffees or coffee styles over and over, and after just two bags, I could tell this would be different.

I set up an order for one 12-oz. bag of whole beans every two weeks. The first bag was Atomic Roasters Space Cadet out of Peabody, MA, and my second bag was Sparrows Coffee, Harmony Series All Seasons Blend from Grand Rapids, MI. I loved the Sparrows bag because it had just enough roast to feel pleasantly dense and weighty on my palate, yet with enough fruit, brightness, and acid to feel lively. When I clicked the box for “medium roast” coffee, this is exactly what I had in mind. I only do pour-over at home, and this was awesome in my Hario V60 coffee dripper.

It has been revealed that recently, senior shopping editor Olivia Tarantino tried Rarities, Trade’s newest program. It’s invite-only, with a rotating lineup of coffees that roasters make as experiments or passion projects. Each coffee is roasted and shipped to order, in batches of a few hundred bags at most. Trade provides detailed instructions direct from the roaster about how to best prepare your beans to get the optimal flavor extraction. She enjoyed an extended fermentation Chiroso variety that had complex acidity of citrus fruits and a slight savory flavor. We haven’t seen anything like Rarities from a subscription service, so serious coffee drinkers should jump on it.

According to recent reports, the bottom line: There is a lot of great coffee in the world, but finding it and getting it right when you want it can be a challenge. Trade takes care of that for you, making this subscription absolutely worth it.

According to recent reports, if you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun fresh seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

In a recent development, testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re a curious coffee connoisseur looking to try single-origin coffee from around the world while directly supporting fair trade and sustainable practices, Atlas is the subscription service for you. Every month, you’ll get a bag of single-origin coffee from a different country that comes with an ID card detailing sourcing information and tasting notes.

Sources indicate that tester: Kelly Janke, former director of culinary production The ordering process was easy. It asked me a few questions about my preferences in roast level, brewing type, and coffee quantity, with options ranging from a half bag to four bags per month. The shipping did seem to take longer than I expected, which was my main qualm with the service.

The beans I received in my first month were medium roast from Rwanda. I really enjoyed the cards that came in the box with tasting notes and information on the growing region. I had chosen two bags per month because I drink a fair amount of coffee, but it’s worth noting that this meant I received two of the same exact coffee (which wasn’t clear at the time of ordering—I had assumed they would be different). I ground the beans in my Oxo burr coffee grinder to a medium grind and brewed them in a Chemex with a metal reusable filter using a 1:16 coffee-to-water ratio. The coffee definitely tasted on the darker side of a medium with notes of grape, red apple, and roasted almonds.

The bottom line: I love to try newly introduced coffee varieties and appreciate the difference; if you feel similarly, then Atlas is a great option for you.

It has been revealed that if you’ve been reading all of this as a decaf drinker, we have good news for you: there are also some great decaf coffee subscriptions out there, including Swiss Water. This subscription offers a rotating selection of decaf coffees from roasters all across the US, all of which have gone through the Swiss Water process, a chemical-free decaffeination technique that you can read more about here. Note that Swiss Water presently only offers whole bean coffees, so you’ll need to grind your own beans if you decide to try it out.

It has been revealed that tester: Alaina Chou I opted for biweekly shipments, though Swiss Water also offers weekly, monthly, and bimonthly. The first coffee I received was from Manzanita Roasting Firm, based in San Diego. There was no informational card included, so all I really gathered about the coffee was that it was from Guatemala and had notes of berries and chocolate, which it did. For a decaf brew, I was impressed by the quality and nuance of the flavor. The same can be stated for the second bag of beans I received, which was a blend called Kick Back from South Carolina–based Barista Alley.

The bottom line: You won’t find the kind of customization and curation options here that you see in most of the other subscriptions on this list, but if you’re okay with trying out a range of decaf coffees and aren’t married to one particular roast level or flavor profile, this service will work for you.

It has been revealed that of every coffee subscription we’ve ever tried, this one is unique. Most coffee beans, even if freshly roasted, are stored as green beans for months. Origin Roasted beans hit the roaster almost immediately after harvest and get shipped out right after that. Truly, they are the freshest coffee beans you can get without picking them yourself. It’s a subjective call as to whether that makes the flavor "better," but it makes it different.

Tester: Noah Kaufman Fruity or chocolate tasting notes that are present in beans that sit green are massively accentuated with Origin Roasted beans. If a flavorful cup of coffee is what you’re after, these beans are as flavorful as they come. The brand’s commitment to roasting at the beans’ origin has the added effect of bringing more coffee roasting work and expertise to countries of origin; roasting for most American coffees happens in the United States.

It has been revealed that the ordering process is straightforward because there are no choices for you to make. Just give them your address and credit card number, and the coffee will be on its way to you at the end of each month. The company only sends the beans it is harvesting that month, which come from a single farm somewhere in Central or South America. The locations are limited to ensure that Origin Roasted can actually get the beans to your door while they’re as fresh as they’re supposed to be.

I got beans from all over Central and South America: Guatemala, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Peru, and Brazil. Each coffee was entirely unlike the one that came before it. Shipments only get sent out on the 28th of every month, so I was limited to one bag per month.

The bottom line: Because of the harvest and roast process, this really is a boutique product, so you can’t order en masse the way you can with larger roasters. I don’t think it makes sense to identify my favorite beans here because you, dear reader, are not guaranteed to get them anyway. What you are guaranteed to get are incredibly cool coffees.

Sources indicate that we are always on the hunt for roasters and subscriptions we haven’t tried. These are the ones that have landed in our grinders recently that we’re loving.

Industry observers note that if you're into the idea of coffee drinking as a ritualistic ~experience~, Folk Coffee Club is for you. Founded by a Q-Grader, a.k.a. a sommelier for the coffee world, Folk specializes in rare coffees that score at least 86 points (in Q-Grader speak). Unlike many of the other coffee subscriptions on this list, Folk gives you zero options; instead, they'll send you one shipment every month with two expert-curated coffees.

It has been revealed that tester: Alaina Chou What really sets Folk apart, though, are the intentional extras they included with each shipment. Along with the two coffees, each month features a piece of art, a curated playlist, some thought starters, and a tasting guide that elevate the mundane ritual of coffee brewing and drinking into a full-blown experience you're encouraged to slow down and savor. The whole package, coffees included, is meant to draw on a unifying theme.

Folk's first shipment, Volume 00, was titled “Off Script,” and featured two Gesha coffees—a distinctive varietal that takes supreme care to grow. Each coffee tasted unlike any other I've had, one with notes of jasmine and caramelized peach, the other reminiscent of blood orange and dark chocolate. The whole thing was beautifully packaged and felt like a luxurious gift to receive, the thoughtful intention behind each component highly evident.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: Think of Folk like a monthly ritual, complete with art, a playlist, and rare coffees you won't find anywhere else. If you're the type to linger over your morning cup, this one's worth every penny.

According to recent reports, there is no better proof point that the world of exquisitely roasted coffee beans has anchored itself absolutely everywhere than the Onyx Coffee Lab. Onyx was started by Jon and Andrea Allen (who would later become a U.S. barista champion) in Springdale, Arkansas, in the Ozarks, and as it has spread throughout the state, it has also become one of the most recognizable names in specialty coffee. Such is Onyx’s reputation that it’s bled over into other areas, landing the Rogers, Arkansas headquarters a nod as a James Beard Award finalist for the best bar program in America.

Tester: Noah Kaufman As for the coffee subscriptions themselves, they’re straightforward to set up: simply tick the box for quantity and the box for frequency. Onyx offers the reliable roaster’s choice option with a lot of interesting single origins and one-offs (I particularly liked a Rwandan washed coffee from Kanzu Station) that all include the most informative explainers I’ve ever seen attached to a bag of coffee. The cards include a breakdown of all the inputs that contribute to the cost, detailed brewing instructions for both pour-over and espresso, and an explanation of the fermentation and roasting process.

In a recent development, for people looking for more familiar flavors, Onyx has subscription options that combine a small amount of more adventurous beans like the Kanzu with its more familiar blends, letting curious drinkers dip their toes in something upcoming. And for a more special experience, Onyx releases a small number of memberships to what it calls “Echelon” for monthly deliveries of its rarest coffee.

Contemporary Coffee Subscription.

In a recent development, the Greenville, South Carolina roaster has grown now to have five cafes, a robust bakery and tea program, and some of the coolest, most beautiful branding in the coffee world. But it also has a wide range of blends and single-producer beans.

According to recent reports, I first walked into Methodical’s café in Greenville in 2017 for a single origin pour-over, and at the time quick national shipping of fresh coffee was still in its early stages, so that stop didn’t end with me signing up for regular deliveries. But now the infrastructure is there and the coffee is great. Methodical sorts its coffee into three main buckets for three different types of coffee drinkers: classic (where you’ll find medium and dark roasts great for batch brewing and espresso), contemporary (where you’ll find medium roast coffees great for batch brewing or pour-over), and “avant-garde” (where you’ll find lighter roast coffees, sometimes fruity, sometimes tea-like, that are best enjoyed black).

Our editors have used every one of these coffee subscriptions in their homes over several months and some for years. We’ve made sure to try a variety of bean types where possible, and to try the beans with a variety of brewing methods to see how well they perform as espresso, pour-over, drip coffee, and French-pressed coffee.

Our editors are continually testing many of these services and constantly trying upcoming coffee subscriptions to keep this list updated as the market changes, so be sure to check back as we upgrade it often.

There are hundreds of coffee subscriptions out there, so we followed two guiding principles when selecting which subscriptions to test:.

A coffee’s freshness has a huge impact on its flavor once brewed, no matter if you’re using a fancy espresso machine or a simple French press. The best subscription services will guarantee freshly roasted beans, either roasted to order or within a week or so of shipping.

The other major factor in your coffee’s flavor is how recently the beans were ground. I’m a substantial advocate of ordering whole-bean coffee and grinding the beans just before brewing, so all of the options we tested offer that. (Of course, I know that many people may prefer the convenience of ground coffee. Most of the services below also offer that as an option, although my colleagues and I will continue to raise our eyebrows at you until you get a good coffee grinder.).

Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor Best for: People who want high-quality coffee, but aren’t interested in choosing from a dizzying array of adventurous options.

It has been revealed that intelligentsia, out of Chicago, is one of the OG players in third-wave coffee (if you’re unfamiliar, "third wave" has a specific meaning, but is sometimes used as shorthand for a generation of coffee roasters deeply invested in quality, consistency, and unique flavors in coffee). Intelligentsia’s House Blend and Black Cat espresso roast have become staples at bakeries and coffee shops all over the country, and its subscription service gives you a regular supply of those two as well as its deeper catalog of different beans. There’s one single origin option, but the subscription itself is mostly based around Intelligentsia’s blends, which rotate seasonally.

This is a pretty simple, straightforward subscription. There is no quiz or process to determine what kind of coffee is “best for you”; rather, you just manually put in which subscription you want, choosing between the same blend (including espresso), rotating blends, or the roaster’s choice. You can also select how many times a month you want beans and how many bags you want per shipment. Changing to a different subscription is also quite easy. While you won’t find the same kind of personalized curation options as some of the other subscriptions on this list, Intelligentsia does offer one of the widest ranges of grind types if you aren’t getting whole bean coffee, running from the finest Turkish coffee grind to a super coarse (even coarser than cold brew) percolator grind.

I got “Intelligentsia's Choice” because I’m a sucker for single-origin beans (and have had the opportunity to try all their classic blends already). The beans came from some of the strongholds of international coffee production: Ethiopia and Nicaragua. Making a carafe of pour-over coffee a day, enough for two people or one me, I used about one bag every two weeks. The most noteworthy coffee to me was a very fruity natural process Ethiopian coffee. After testing it extensively, I can tell you that this is a reliable, relatively affordable subscription; the Intelligentsia Classics subscription is only $17 a bag. It would be worthwhile for anyone who wants quality but isn’t trying to be too adventurous with their morning coffee.

Just to note, in 2015, Peet’s bought up a majority stake in Intelligentsia. I don’t think it has changed the quality of the coffee at all, but it is something worth being transparent about.

Tester: Carly Westerfield, associate manager of audience strategy Best for: Someone who likes high-quality beans and doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for, but might get overwhelmed by some of the multi-roaster options on this list.

Recent findings suggest that counter Culture is a longtime favorite roaster of many a BA staffer (food director Chris Morocco included). It has storefronts in several major cities, and you can find Counter Culture’s coffee in stores across the country, but they also offer several subscription options online.

I had a really easy time ordering the coffee. There aren’t endless options to choose from, which is nice because subscriptions like these can sometimes be a lot to manage. Because I wanted to see a variety of beans, there were only two: the Single-Origin Subscription and the Blend Box. I opted for the latter. As someone who’s often overwhelmed by choices, I always appreciate a curated shopping experience where there are fewer things to choose from and therefore fewer things to compare, contrast, and potentially have buyer’s remorse over. I did struggle a little to figure out how to end the subscription; Counter Culture makes that part a little trickier than everything else.

Recent findings suggest that this subscription sends two different blends (12-oz. bags) at a time at a frequency of your choosing. Options there ranged from every week to every eight weeks, and the ability to change this post-purchase was clear. The Blend Box subscription pulls from six blend options ranging from light to dark roast, plus any “seasonal blend’ they have available, so you will end up seeing the same beans after about four deliveries. Shipping was fast and the email communication from CC made it so I always knew when I was being charged and when the box would be shipped and delivered.

While trying out this subscription, I received four different coffee blends: Iridescent Winter Blend, Big Trouble, Fast Forward, and Forty-Six. At home, I use a Moccamaster Thermal Carafe Coffee Brewer and a Baratza Encore Coffee Grinder. With each of the blends I received, I was able to use the same measurements that I always use (9 g of coffee per 6 oz. of water) and found the coffee to be the right strength for me. Each blend has spot-on tasting notes provided as well. Overall, while the flavor profiles were totally different, none were overwhelmingly bitter or acidic—a big no-no in my book. These coffees all had a really well-rounded, almost creamy quality to them that actually resulted in me using way less half-and-half than I normally take in my coffee. By far my favorite blend is, sadly, the limited edition Iridescent Winter Blend. Big Trouble came in a close second.

This subscription is great for someone who likes high-quality beans but doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for—perhaps, for instance, a recent college grad who’s been drinking coffee for years but hasn’t had to buy it for their own home yet. The ability to pause or change how often the deliveries come also makes it nice for someone who might travel often or need to have more coffee on hand at random times (maybe they have frequent house guests?).

Tester: Maria Paz Mendez Hodes, director of creative development Best for: Eager-to-learn beginners.

Sources indicate that stumptown is a Portland, OR–based roaster that’s been around since 1999. It offers three subscription options: Roaster’s Choice, Blend Shuffle, and Favorite on Repeat. As a novice coffee brewer, I wished there were a little more elaboration on the differences between Roaster’s Choice and Blend Shuffle. In the end I opted for the Roaster’s Choice, which promised to be a tour of seasonal, single-origin, and occasionally rare coffees, changing every two weeks.

Sources indicate that I wasn’t 100% sure until the bag showed up at my door that I was ordering whole beans versus ground coffee. To some that may be glaringly obvious, but just another reminder that the site did not seem aimed at rank beginners like me. From what I can tell, Stumptown subscriptions are all whole-bean-only. Beyond that, the ordering process was clear and easy! My first bag arrived three days after ordering, and the next one almost exactly on schedule.

A guilty confession: We keep breaking the Hario V60 carafe that I use to make pour-over, and I’ve gotten hooked on the extravagant convenience of bottled cold brew. The arrival of the Stumptown beans was exciting enough that we couldn’t wait for a replacement to arrive from Amazon, so we improvised by setting the dripper over a mason jar. Unglamorous setup aside, the first brew was an immediate reminder of the sense pleasures of the morning coffee ritual, dramatically amplified by using the fanciest beans I’d ever purchased. The freshness of the seasonal beans was obvious upon opening the package—they were lustrous and almost oily, with juicy notes that I’ve rarely detected in the supermarket brands near me. I don’t have a highly attuned coffee nose, but I could certainly taste distinct differences between the bags I received: light, bright fruit in the Montes de Oro from Costa Rica and deep caramel and spice in the Duramina from Ethiopia.

According to recent reports, there were blurbs on the back of each bag sketching details about the coffee producers (e.g., how long they’d partnered with Stumptown and some unique features of their agricultural operations). It’s a good initiation for an interested newbie, but I think a coffee enthusiast could still glean quite a bit from these brief details. The one addition I would have loved would have been a card in the box with some deeper insights connecting the tasting notes and flavors to the processes and places mentioned. While there were tasting notes on the website for “Pick of the Week,” the coffee described wasn’t one I had received—another argument for a card in the box.

Tester: Travis Rainey, staff photographer/visuals editor Best for: People who like a little personality in their morning coffee.

According to recent reports, I was tempted to choose a curveball and select the espresso subscription, but opted for a more American coffee experience this time. I chose to test the Curated Single Origin subscription, which sends you a different single-origin coffee bean each week. The first bag of beans I received was from Concepción Huista, just north of Huehuetenango in western Guatemala. It was a very light, almost delicate kind of coffee. I had to adjust the grinder setting to a finer coffee ground to make the coffee a little more bold. For the most part, I make coffee with a pour-over method. A newly introduced coffee arrives each week, so the next selection was from Abana Estate near Jimma in southwestern Ethiopia. This has been my favorite coffee to make so far. It's distinctive, spiced, but still goes down smooth. The third variety is Panangan Mata from Aceh on the northern tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. I’ve only had one cup yet, but it’s fruity, which is a fun surprise.

In general, I’ve found that each Equator coffee has had a distinct personality, making this subscription ideal for people who want to have opinions about coffee—the beans here are the kind that sort of demand one of you. I also appreciate that the containers the coffee beans come in feature detailed, but succinct information on where the coffee is coming from.

Tester: Hana Asbrink, deputy food director Best for: Both novice and experienced coffee drinkers alike who want their coffee selections handled for them.

Sources indicate that my ordering experience was straightforward. I chose the Roaster’s Choice Subscription, so I didn’t know what I’d be getting first. My first bag (Honduras San Francisco whole beans) had a roast date just three days before it arrived at my house, so you can’t get much fresher than that. I appreciated this first blind bean as I’m not sure I would have chosen it for myself based on my personal preferences. I used a medium grind on the whole beans for my drip coffee maker. I’m curious to see how I’ll enjoy it pulled in the big boy coffee maker as an Americano.

The bag touts tasting notes of strawberry, raspberry, and dark chocolate, which are spot-on. The first whiff gave me a fruit-and-nut chocolate bar, and the taste matches in a delicate way with a touch some floral undertones.

Tester: Carina Finn Best for: Best for someone with a high-end caffeine routine.

In a recent development, you can find a Blue Bottle café in most major cities—the brand makes a reliably great cup of coffee, whether you’re into fruity pour-overs or sophisticated seasonal lattes. Blue Bottle’s coffee subscription makes it easy to recreate that experience at home. It has around 10 different subscription options for things like instant espresso and matcha powders to rotating single-origin offerings and subscriptions tailored to specific roast level preferences.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: Someone looking for seasonality in their coffee.

It has been revealed that sightglass is a coffee-shop-slash-roaster based in San Francisco. They offer subscriptions for all of the coffees in their regular lineup if you find a fave you want to stick to, but we’d recommend trying out one of their rotating options to get a taste for all the brand has to offer. That leaves you with either the Blend Shuffle or the Seasonal Variety subscription. The ordering process is simple: Just select which subscription you want, how much coffee you want in each shipment (12 ounces, 2 pounds, or 5 pounds), what kind of grind you want, and how often you’d like to receive deliveries.

One of the things I like about Sightglass, as opposed to some other coffee shop-roaster hybrids, is that they regularly introduce newly introduced single-origin coffees, which might feature in that seasonal subscription. You can also opt in to get notified about any new drops through the Sightglass Batches text-to-order service.

It has been revealed that I'm partial to Sightglass’s Blueboon blend. It's a medium roast with notes of milk chocolate, mandarin, and honeysuckle that I quite enjoy brewed as espresso and used in my morning iced latte. It’s beautifully balanced, and the components get changed seasonally to retain the right ratio of sweetness, body, and acidity.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: People who want to hone their coffee-tasting skills.

In a recent development, if you dream of being able to approach the coffee world with sommelier-like expertise but you aren’t quite there yet, a Driftaway coffee subscription will help. Driftaway is an immigrant-owned, woman-led roastery based in Brooklyn, NY, and it’s the only service we’ve tried that starts out with a blind tasting. When you go to place your first order, you’ll have the option to choose between light roast, medium, and dark roasts, or espresso (which each include two or three different 4-oz. bags of coffee to blind taste test), or opt for the Explorer Box, which includes five different coffees spanning all roast levels.

Sources indicate that if the tasting aspect of this service appeals to you, I’d recommend going with the Explorer Box option. Each initial Explorer Box comes with five mystery coffees, a wheel with flavor notes, a tasting form, and an envelope revealing the identities of your coffees. Driftaway offers weekly virtual tasting classes free of charge, but if you’d rather taste on your own time, they also have prerecorded tasting tutorials available on their website. Regardless of whether you opt for the Explorer Box or a roast-specific subscription, after your initial order, you’ll give feedback on which coffee you preferred in order to inform your future shipments. Many coffee companies even give you the option to send the farmer feedback, which I appreciated.

Recent findings suggest that along with the Explorer Box, I also tried out the espresso subscription. I was partial to the Burundi Turihamwe and Guatemala Ella blend, which was wonderfully nutty and had notes of milk chocolate and stone fruits. I loved being able to read more about the women farmers behind this blend and trace the story of the coffee from harvest to brewing, a feature that’s in keeping with Driftaway’s overall ethos.

Founded in 2015 in NYC's East Village, Coffee Project NY has grown from a single café into a full operation spanning retail, roasting, wholesale, and education. Owner Chi Sum Ngai is a certified Q grader and roasting championship competitor who personally oversees the roasting program, sourcing from small-scale cooperatives and family farms committed to improving conditions for workers.

In a recent development, tester: Olivia Tarantino, senior commerce editor The subscription is straightforward: select the Roaster's Choice Single Origin Subscription and receive one to three 10-oz. bags one to two times a month. Coffee Project New York is not shy about its credentials; each bag arrives with tasting notes, farm sourcing, processing methods, and MASL (metres above sea level, which indicates the altitude at which beans were grown and profoundly impacts flavor). My standout was the Cabra Noir Wush Wush from the Competition Series, a runner-up at Mexico's prestigious AMCCE competition. Produced through anaerobic fermentation, I hand-ground the beans for a Hario pour-over and was met with such vivid guava notes that I double-checked the bag to make sure it wasn't a cofermentation. It wasn't. It was just that good.

Bottom line: Any coffee drinker will appreciate the expertly sourced beans, but this is a subscription where nerds can truly geek out, sampling rare cultivars and competition-level coffees from around the world.

Wonderstate Coffee (Single Origin).

Wonderstate Coffee Blend Shuffle).

Wonderstate Coffee (Roaster's Choice).

A certified B-Corporation with a fully solar-powered roastery, a transparent farmer payment model, and a novel profit-sharing model, Viroqua-based Wonderstate has gained a lot of goodwill for its business practices, but it also makes really good coffee.

Sources indicate that tester: Noah Kaufman Admittedly, this is a bit of a homer pick, as I have long thought Wonderstate to be the preeminent coffee roaster from my beloved home state of Wisconsin. But for those of you not lucky enough to be from Wisconsin, you should get to know them too. Twice named roaster of the year by Roast magazine (which is probably how it ended up as part of the Podium Coffee subscription), Wonderstate regularly has delicious, clean limited edition single origins—I like to get them as part of the single origin flight subscription. The subscriptions themselves come in a few varieties. The single-origin flight delivers three 100-gram packages of Wonderstate’s rarer coffees every two weeks. Roaster’s choice delivers a different single-origin coffee at an interval of your choosing. And the single coffee subscription gives you a regular delivery of the Wonderstate blend of your choosing, if you’re the type who wants more consistency of flavor in your morning cup.

Recent findings suggest that the bottom line: Wonderstate makes excellent coffee and runs an ethical business, which is a combination that's rarer than it should be. If you care about where your money goes as much as what's in your cup, this is the subscription for you.

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Specialty Subscription).

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Year Round Subscription).

According to recent reports, if you find most black coffee off-putting, you might still love an unadulterated cup from Raleigh, North Carolina’s Black and White Coffee Roasters. Started by two American barista champions, Black and White are masters of the funky and fruity, with lots of experiments in co-fermented coffee (a process that uses actual fruit) and anaerobic fermented coffee (which produces very pronounced fruit notes).

According to recent reports, tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor It can be a very hands-off subscription. The only required information is whether you want one or two bags at a time and the frequency you need your coffee (anywhere between one and six weeks). Black and White will take care of the rest. If you do see a bag on their website you like, you can add it to your queue; otherwise, the team in North Carolina will select for you.

Every bag I received was of a funky variety, using ingredients like passion fruit, but they produce a number of more classic flavor profiles, which are available as part of their “year-round” subscription; the year-round is also about 20% cheaper than a subscription with the specialty bags.

Sources indicate that the bottom line: If you're drawn to funky, fruit-forward coffee but don't want to think too hard about what to order next, Black and White is the subscription for you. Just set your frequency and let the barista champions decide.

Sources indicate that bean Box is focused on the “curation” experience. The service’s tasting team offers what they claim is the largest selection of specialty coffee online, with over 600 different brews in its rolodex. The selection is sourced from dozens of small-batch, sustainably focused roasters from around the country—meaning you could likely go years without tasting coffee from the same roaster twice.

Sources indicate that tester: Dan Siegel, head of video Starting my subscription was exceptionally easy and clear. I appreciated the option to tailor the subscription to my own tastes: Bean Box asked me to choose among Light & Bright, Medium & Cozy, Dark & Toasty, Espresso, or Decaf. For this run, I selected the Curators' Choice option, marketed as the curation team’s seasonal favorites and a mix of newly introduced and old coffees. There is an app available to manage subscriptions and read lengthy details on each roaster or track the origin of your beans.

It has been revealed that this subscription was not designed to save me money on coffee; this is for enthusiasts. My first bag from “Gimme! Coffee,” out of Ithaca, NY, hit hard on the Bean Box mission: The roaster is employee-owned, shipping fair trade beans from Coopfam, Brazil’s first certified fair trade coffee grower. This was a standout for any time of day as a medium-bodied brew, subtly sweet with virtually no bitterness or acidity via my automatic OXO 8-cup machine or my Hario V60 pour-over. My second bag, La Cumbre from Little City in Austin, was a bit too bright and fruity for my taste, advertising caramel, mango, and green apple tasting notes—but this was the path I chose with the Curator’s Choice option.

Sources indicate that the bottom line: If you have the means, get the beans. I would keep this going for years if money were no object. The money seems to be going toward roasters that align with my values. One of my values is delicious coffee. But also treating workers at every stop along the way like human beings.

If receiving personalized coffee picks from a catalogue of nearly 600 coffees from 60 different roasters sounds like your cup of tea (or, rather, joe), then I will point you toward MistoBox. I found a lot to love about this service after testing it for several months, particularly the way Misto tailored its selections to me and my taste.

According to recent reports, tester: Alaina Chou, commerce writer The ordering process starts with a quiz covering your preferences: how you take your coffee, roast level, whole or ground beans, and frequency. But what sets MistoBox apart is what comes after: a second, more detailed quiz where you share how you brew, how you grind, and any other specifics to help the team dial in your order. The whole process feels genuinely personal, and that expert-curated aspect is, to me, the other major perk that makes a subscription worth it in the first place.

In a recent development, I’ve loved every coffee MistoBox has sent me so far. The first shipment was the Roma Espresso Blend from Parisi Artisan Coffee, which was aptly described as having notes of milk chocolate, almond, and honeysuckle. I tend to drink espresso, most often with milk in a cappuccino made using my Breville Oracle Jet. The Roma blend, which MistoBox sent me based on that information, worked beautifully for this.

After you receive each coffee, you’ll have the chance to rate it out of five and leave any tasting notes, which you can share with your curators if you’d like. Coffees you’ve tried show up in a customer dashboard, as will your “Brew Queue,” a.k.a. the lineup of the next coffees coming to your door. These will appear as “MistoBox’s choice” by default, but if you loved a coffee you tried and want it again, or spy a coffee in their collection that you’d like to request, you can opt to add specific coffees to your queue as well. Anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering newly introduced coffees from roasters all over the country will enjoy MistoBox.

The bottom line: MistoBox’s user-friendly interface and extensive feedback options make it a great choice for anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering newly introduced coffees from roasters all over the country.

Are coffee subscriptions worth it?

If you’re a frequent coffee drinker, the answer is probably yes. Whether you have a favorite blend you find yourself buying on repeat or you’re eager to try fresh beans and hone your tasting skills, a coffee subscription will make your life easier and may even save you some money. If you’re right now buying a bag of beans every few weeks at your local coffee shop or grocery store, that bag could potentially be cheaper when bought on subscription—and you’ll get the added convenience of never needing to worry about restocking your stash.

How do coffee subscriptions work?

At the most basic level, a coffee subscription works much like any other subscription service: You select a quantity and frequency, and lo and behold, a bag of freshly roasted coffee shows up at your doorstep every one to four weeks, depending what you chose. But no one wants to come home from vacation to a pile of beans that are past their prime, only to receive another package the following day. So these coffee subscriptions make it easy to put your coffee deliveries on hold, or cancel them altogether. Some also offer personalization in the form of quizzes or feedback forms, so you can know you're getting a curated selection that’s tailored specifically to your tastes.

How much coffee should you order?

According to recent reports, many of the subscriptions on this list will let you customize your delivery frequency and bag quantity to best accommodate your household size and coffee drinking habits. Ideally, you’ll want to hit a sweet spot where you're using up nearly all of your beans by the time the next shipment comes. To figure out the right amount of coffee for you, you’ll need to do a little math:.

If instant coffee is more your speed, we don’t blame you—it’s hard to beat the convenience. And while instant coffee has historically gotten a bad wrap from third-wave coffee nerds and espresso heads everywhere, you’d be surprised what innovations have been made in the space in recent years. After tasting a whopping 40, we found a range of great-tasting options that would impress even the most seasoned coffee pro. Head this way for our review of all the best instant coffees and espressos money can buy.

Now that you’ve read all about the best coffee subscription services out there, it’s time to upgrade that old drip coffee machine or invest in a upcoming espresso setup.

The Best Holiday Cocktails, According to Eater Editors
