Euclid's Hunt for Strong Gravitational Lenses is Off to a Strong Start

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness.
  • Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns.
  • One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

Industry observers note that this artist's illustration highlights the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

Dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

It has been revealed that dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â stated Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

This image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and reveals the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

In a recent development, euclid rolled out in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Major Bang.

Among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

According to recent reports, euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 new strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

According to recent reports, "Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â said Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 new candidates.â.

It has been revealed that there's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row shows, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

According to recent reports, overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â remarked Srivastava.

Strong gravitational lensing is an crucial tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

Finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly important in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang model of cosmology.

According to recent reports, lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Industry observers note that euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one big grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each new data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

Industry observers note that but that won't be the end of cosmology. Newly introduced questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

#54272. Scientists Solve a Longstanding Mystery About the Tiny Gateways That Protect Our DNA

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists Solve a Longstanding Mystery About the Tiny Gateways That Protect Our DNA

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.
  • Every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored.
  • “As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most vital molecular machines in the human cell,” said Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a newly introduced study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.

Every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored. Known as nuclear pores, these openings allow certain molecules to enter or leave while blocking others. Scientists have long understood the structure of these gateways, yet the proteins controlling what gets through have remained a mystery. Do they form a rigid barrier, or something more like a constantly shifting liquid?

“As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most vital molecular machines in the human cell,” said Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a newly introduced study published in Nature. “And also one of the most complex,” added co-first author Maziar Heidari of the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany.

Much of the uncertainty comes from how differently these proteins behave outside living cells. Previous experiments with isolated proteins produced everything from stretched chains to liquid-like droplets and thick gels resembling gummy bears. Some even formed solid deposits.

However, those observations could not establish what happens inside an actual nuclear pore, where thousands of molecular interactions help control traffic. “Such studies did not, however, allow any direct conclusions to be drawn about how the barrier behaves within the living cell,” remarked Professor Edward Lemke, Professor of Synthetic Biophysics at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU).

To investigate the barrier in its natural environment, Lemke and his colleagues attached fluorescent dyes to proteins inside the nuclear pores of living cells. These tiny glowing markers allowed the researchers to track protein movement and determine how flexible the barrier remained. The proteins moved rapidly throughout the entire two-hour observation period, indicating that the interior of the pore behaves more like a fluid than a solid.

Sources indicate that “For the first time, we have been able to measure intrinsic protein dynamics within the nanocanal of a living cell and demonstrate that the interior of this canal is fluid-like,” said Lemke, who led the study alongside Professor Gerhard Hummer of MPI-BP. “As the dyes move extremely quickly, the state inside the nuclear pores must be fluid-like,” he explained.

It has been revealed that the contrast became clearer when the researchers compared their observations with proteins isolated in a test tube. After approximately two hours, the protein material consistently hardened into a gummy-bear-like gel or an even more rigid solid. Some of these deposits resembled protein accumulations associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Inside living cells, however, the barrier remained flexible over the same period. “This was a crucial turning point: there had to be something keeping the barrier in the cells dynamic,” noted Lemke.

Industry observers note that the researchers identified two components that helped explain the difference. One was a transport receptor, a protein involved in moving molecules through nuclear pores. The other was glycosylation, a process that attaches sugar groups to proteins and helps prevent them from sticking together too tightly. When both were included in the laboratory model, the proteins regained much of the mobility observed in living cells. “When we add these two components, we observe a similar mobility in the model system to that found in the nuclear pores of living cells,” said Lemke.

It has been revealed that understanding the barrier’s flexibility also helped the team tackle another longstanding puzzle: where molecules actually travel as they pass through the pore. In an ordinary pipe or river, flow is generally fastest near the center and slower along the edges. Earlier research suggested that nuclear pores work differently, with much of the transport occurring near their outer walls. One proposed explanation was that a biological structure, possibly a plug, occupied the middle and forced molecules toward the sides.

Hummer’s team investigated this possibility using what the researchers describe as the most comprehensive simulation model of a nuclear pore developed to date. The model incorporated experimental measurements from the Mainz team, including how extensively the barrier proteins were linked to one another. It allowed the researchers to examine how molecules would move through a pore with the physical properties they had measured.

“The simulations confirm that the main transport route runs along the edge of the pore,” said Hummer. Importantly, the calculations demonstrated that this pattern could emerge from the pore’s physical and chemical properties without requiring a central obstruction. “While we do not rule out a biological cause such as a plug, it is not necessary from a physicochemical point of view.”.

Industry observers note that producing such a detailed model required enormous computing power. “These complex calculations were made possible by JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer at the Jülich Research Center,” stated Hummer.

The experiments and simulations provide a clearer picture of how nuclear pores maintain a flexible barrier while regulating the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus. They may also help researchers investigate why proteins that normally remain flexible sometimes harden into deposits, a process involved in neurodegenerative diseases.

In a recent development, reference: “Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores” by Miao Yu (于淼), Maziar Heidari, Karen Palacio-Rodriguez, Hao Ruan (阮浩), Sara Mingu, Yu Chen (陈宇), Xu-Zhuo Gou (缑绪卓), Pingkai Shen (沈平恺), Songzi Liu (刘松子), Si-Yu Chen (陈思宇), Alam Ahmad Hidayat, Mathis Bode, Mateusz Sikora, Ai-Hui Tang (唐爱辉), Gerhard Hummer and Edward A. Lemke, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • It has been revealed that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • In a recent development, to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

It has been revealed that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

In a recent development, to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

In the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

Industry observers note that but why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

But ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision.

#54268. Industry News: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

Industry News: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1451 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • According to recent reports, earth is one big system.
  • Industry observers note that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a big part of understanding the present-day Earth.

According to recent reports, earth is one big system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a upcoming trick with them: photosynthesis.

Industry observers note that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

Recent findings suggest that but this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

It has been revealed that latest research in The Innovation indicates how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

The oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research shows that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on new geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

Recent findings suggest that they found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

Recent findings suggest that the second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

The researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

Industry observers note that this graphic illustrates the results from newly introduced research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that highlights how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Sources indicate that on shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it shows that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

Sources indicate that "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

Sources indicate that this figure highlights the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Recent findings suggest that it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work shows that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

Sources indicate that the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

According to recent reports, understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District.
  • Sources indicate that north Carolina Rep.
  • Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that north Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”.

Sources indicate that hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, Latest York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Sources indicate that republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a latest GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

In a recent development, north Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

In a recent development, “We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”.

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

Recent findings suggest that as a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

Experimental Drug Wipes Out Aggressive Pancreatic Cancer in 75% of Mice and Triggers Lasting Immunity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An experimental drug helped mice resist cancers their immune systems had never encountered, raising the possibility that treating one tumor could someday help protect against others.
  • Sources indicate that pancreatic cancer remains one of the most difficult cancers to treat, partly because tumors can wall themselves off from the immune system.
  • Researchers have now developed an experimental drug that breaks through this barrier in mice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An experimental drug helped mice resist cancers their immune systems had never encountered, raising the possibility that treating one tumor could someday help protect against others.

Sources indicate that pancreatic cancer remains one of the most difficult cancers to treat, partly because tumors can wall themselves off from the immune system. Many breast, colon, and lung cancers use the same defense, surrounding themselves with dense, scar-like tissue that keeps cancer-fighting immune cells out. This barrier is one reason immunotherapy, which helps the immune system attack cancer, works for only a minority of patients with solid tumors.

Researchers have now developed an experimental drug that breaks through this barrier in mice. The treatment eliminated aggressive pancreatic tumors in some animals, prevented breast cancer from spreading, and produced lasting immune protection against future cancers.

The study, published November 9, 2026, in Cancer Cell, was led by Seong-Jin Kim, PhD, and scientists at MedPacto, Inc., in Seoul, Korea.

Tumors build their defenses partly by releasing large amounts of a chemical messenger called TGF-β. This substance encourages nearby cells to produce fibrous tissue while weakening the immune cells that could attack the cancer. Blocking it has proven difficult because TGF-β also performs notable functions in healthy tissue. Previous drugs have struggled to suppress enough of it inside tumors without causing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

In a recent development, to get around this problem, the team developed a drug called FEBP-sTβRII that carries a molecular tag directing it toward tumors. The tag attaches to a particular form of fibronectin, a protein abundant in many cancers but rarely found in healthy adult tissue. Researchers detected this target in mouse models of breast, colon, lung, liver, prostate, pancreatic, and brain cancers, as well as melanoma, and in many human tumor types.

The targeted drug accumulated inside tumors and remained there for days. Without the tag, the same blocker had little effect on tumors and altered the activity of 693 genes in the blood, compared with just 25 for the targeted treatment.

“This study shows that where you block TGF-β matters as much as whether you block it,” mentioned senior author Kim, who is also affiliated with the GILO Institute.

With the protective barrier weakened, cancer-killing T cells could enter the tumors. They released a chemical signal called interferon-gamma, prompting nearby support cells and immune cells to display recognizable pieces of the cancer. This helped the immune system identify its target and sustain the attack. Researchers observed this response in pancreatic tumors and melanoma.

Unlike existing immunotherapies that primarily remove restrictions on T cells, the experimental drug also changes the environment surrounding the cancer, making it easier for immune cells to reach and recognize tumors.

The researchers reported several promising results across different mouse experiments:.

“TGF-β helps build the defenses of many solid tumors, so this approach has the potential to reach well beyond a single cancer,” remarked Dr. Letterio. “By delivering the blocker directly to the tumor, we don’t just open the door to T cells. We appear to be teaching the immune system lessons it remembers long after the tumor is gone, and in some cases those lessons protect against other cancers.”.

In a recent development, study co-author John J. Letterio, MD, PhD, directs the Angie Fowler Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Institute at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies & Children’s Hospital and the Developmental Therapeutics Program at Case Comprehensive Cancer Center, Case Western Reserve University.

Recent findings suggest that the immune response observed in mice resembled patterns previously seen in patients who responded to immunotherapy for melanoma, gastric cancer, and pancreatic cancer. Measuring the drug’s fibronectin target in tumors might eventually help identify patients most likely to benefit.

A human version of the drug has entered safety testing, with clinical trials planned for 2027 to evaluate its safety and effectiveness in patients whose solid tumors have not responded to standard treatments.

In a recent development, reference: “A stroma-sensing TGF-β blockade reprograms CAF-myeloid niches to induce durable tumor immunity” by Dong Woo Kang, Jin Beom Bae, Seonho Yoo, Hyejin Kim, Pyunggang Kim, Jaewoo Mo, Jinhwan Kim, Jin Su Kim, Kwiyeom Yoon, Ye Seon Kim, Jeong Su Lee, June Myoung Kim, Min Gi Kang, Min Jung Lee, Changwon Lim, Isaac Y. Kim, Chang Pyo Hong, Junil Kim, John J. Letterio and Seong-Jin Kim, 09 November 2026, Cancer Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.ccell.2026.10.007.

Recent findings suggest that disclosure: Dr. Kim is a founder of MedPacto and co-founder of Celloram. Dr. Letterio is a co-founder of Celloram and a member of MedPacto’s clinical advisory board. MedPacto holds pending patents on the drug.

Why Sleeping 9 Hours After 50 May Be a Warning Sign for Your Career

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More sleep does not necessarily mean more years at work, as a large Finnish study links both restless nights and unusually long sleep to shorter working lives.
  • Industry observers note that as retirement ages rise and people are expected to work later into life, researchers are looking more closely at what helps people remain in the workforce as they grow older.
  • Sources indicate that people with severe sleep disturbances could expect to spend around eight fewer months in the workforce than those who rarely experienced sleep problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More sleep does not necessarily mean more years at work, as a large Finnish study links both restless nights and unusually long sleep to shorter working lives.

Industry observers note that as retirement ages rise and people are expected to work later into life, researchers are looking more closely at what helps people remain in the workforce as they grow older. A large Finnish study suggests that sleep may be part of the picture. Adults who frequently struggled with sleep after age 50 tended to spend fewer years working, while those who regularly slept nine hours or more a night also had shorter expected working lives.

Sources indicate that people with severe sleep disturbances could expect to spend around eight fewer months in the workforce than those who rarely experienced sleep problems. Among people who slept at least nine hours a night, the gap ranged from roughly nine months to more than two years, depending on the study group.

The findings, published online in Occupational & Environmental Medicine, come as more than half of the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) have raised statutory retirement ages in response to aging populations. Previous research has explored why people leave their jobs early, including disability, illness, and retirement decisions. However, researchers had not examined whether sleep duration and quality were associated with how long people remain employed.

To investigate, the team focused on working life expectancy, which measures the average number of years someone can expect to remain employed at a particular age. Rather than measuring how long people live, the researchers examined their expected years in the workforce between ages 50 and 68.

The analysis drew on two Finnish studies involving more than 76,000 adults. The Finnish Public Sector (FPS) study included 70,339 public sector employees between 2000 and 2016, approximately 80% of whom were women. The Health and Social Support (HeSSup) study provided a random sample of 6,071 working-age Finnish adults between 1998 and 2013, with women accounting for 54% of participants. Researchers assessed sleep using the first survey each participant completed after turning 50, then examined employment information from the Earnings and Accrual Register, maintained by the Finnish Centre for Pensions.

The surveys asked participants how long they usually slept and how often they experienced difficulties falling asleep, staying asleep, waking too early, or feeling unrested after sleeping. These disturbances were assessed over the preceding four weeks. People who experienced them no more than once a week were considered to have no sleep disturbances, while those reporting problems two to four nights a week were placed in the moderate category. Severe disturbances meant experiencing these problems five or six nights a week to nearly every night. Sleep duration was classified separately as short, meaning less than seven hours, mid-range at seven to eight and a half hours, or long at nine hours or more.

The results revealed a consistent relationship between disrupted sleep and fewer expected years of employment. Participants without sleep disturbances had an average working life expectancy of 13 years and five months after age 50. That fell to approximately 13 years among those with moderate disturbances and 12 years and 10 months among those with severe problems. Compared with people reporting no disturbances, these groups could expect to work nearly five and eight fewer months, respectively. The association appeared among both men and women and across three broad occupational categories: professional, intermediate, and routine jobs.

Sources indicate that employment differences became more apparent when researchers examined sleep alongside occupation and sex. Professional women who reported no sleep disturbances had the longest expected working lives in this comparison, at nearly 14 years after age 50. Men in routine jobs who experienced severe sleep disturbances had the shortest, at approximately 12 and a half years.

Sleep duration revealed a somewhat different pattern. In the Finnish Public Sector study, participants sleeping fewer than seven hours a night and those sleeping between seven and eight and a half hours had the same average working life expectancy of 13 years and two months. Those who regularly slept nine hours or more, however, had an expected working life of just 12 years and five months. Compared with the mid-range sleep group, that represented approximately nine fewer months of employment.

In a recent development, the association was even stronger in the HeSSup study, where sleeping nine hours or more was linked to just over 30 fewer months of expected employment compared with sleeping seven to eight and a half hours. Researchers found no clear evidence that people sleeping fewer than seven hours had shorter working lives than those in the mid-range category, regardless of sex or job type.

Sources indicate that education and occupation also appeared to shape these patterns. When researchers compared the most advantaged participants, those with professional jobs or higher education and no sleep disturbances or short to mid-range sleep, with the least advantaged, those in routine jobs or with lower education and severe sleep problems or long sleep, the differences were considerable. The gap in expected working life was approximately one year and five months in the FPS group and five years in the HeSSup group.

According to recent reports, in a more detailed analysis combining sleep duration with socioeconomic circumstances, 50-year-old men and women in professional jobs who reported short nightly sleep had the longest expected working lives in the FPS study, at around 13 years and seven months. In HeSSup, highly educated women had the longest working life expectancy, at approximately 11 and a half years. At the other extreme, men in routine jobs or with lower levels of education who regularly slept nine hours or more had an expected working life of only about six years and five months in both study groups.

According to recent reports, although the findings suggest a connection between sleep and working life, they do not establish that poor sleep or longer sleep directly causes people to leave employment earlier. The study was observational, and the researchers could not account for several potentially influential factors, including physical and mental health, underlying medical conditions, risky health behaviors, and working conditions such as shift work. These factors could affect both sleep patterns and the ability to remain employed.

Still, the findings suggest that helping people manage sleep problems in midlife may be worth considering as countries look for ways to support longer working careers, particularly among people facing socioeconomic disadvantages.

“Promoting sleep health and providing support for managing sleep disturbances at midlife may be especially notable for those with a lower socioeconomic status when aiming to increase workforce participation with advancing age,” the researchers concluded.

“This could include cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia delivered by occupational health services or workplace interventions, such as educational or health promotion interventions for sleep.”.

Reference: “Sleep disturbances and sleep duration as predictors of working life expectancy among adults aged 50 years and older in Finland” by Saana Myllyntausta, Katriina Heikkilä, Jaana Pentti, Holendro Singh Chungkham, Sakari Suominen, Mika Kivimaki, Jussi Vahtera, Paola Zaninotto, Jenni Ervasti and Sari Stenholm, 18 August 2026, Occupational and Environmental Medicine. DOI: 10.1136/oemed-2025-110766.

#54261. Breaking: New FDA-Approved Pill Lowers High Blood Pressure and May Slow Kidney Disease

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (933 w)

Breaking: New FDA-Approved Pill Lowers High Blood Pressure and May Slow Kidney Disease

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced drug targeting a hormone linked to hypertension has shown encouraging results in patients with chronic kidney disease.
  • A drug that showed early signs of protecting damaged kidneys has now received FDA approval for treating high blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite medication.
  • According to recent reports, the approval follows Phase 3 clinical trials showing substantial blood pressure reductions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced drug targeting a hormone linked to hypertension has shown encouraging results in patients with chronic kidney disease.

A drug that showed early signs of protecting damaged kidneys has now received FDA approval for treating high blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite medication. Called Baxfendy (baxdrostat), the treatment targets a hormone involved in both hypertension and kidney disease.

According to recent reports, the approval follows Phase 3 clinical trials showing substantial blood pressure reductions. Earlier research also found that baxdrostat lowered a key marker of kidney damage by 55%, suggesting potential benefits beyond hypertension. Whether the medication can slow kidney disease progression remains under investigation.

In a recent development, the FDA approved AstraZeneca’s Baxfendy in May 2026 for adults whose hypertension remains inadequately controlled by existing treatments. It is the first approved aldosterone synthase inhibitor, a class of drugs that reduces production of the hormone aldosterone.

In the Phase 3 BaxHTN trial involving 796 patients, the 2 mg dose reduced systolic blood pressure by an average of 15.7 mm Hg after 12 weeks, compared with 5.8 mm Hg for placebo. The additional reduction of 9.8 mm Hg was statistically significant. A lower 1 mg dose also produced meaningful improvements.

Sources indicate that dr. Bryan Williams, Chair of Medicine at University College London and the trial’s primary investigator, said: “We have been waiting for an innovative medication like Baxfendy for hypertension for many years. Its novel way of lowering blood pressure has the potential to transform clinical practice by targeting a root cause of persistently uncontrolled hypertension. In addition, the nearly double-digit placebo-adjusted systolic blood pressure reduction achieved with Baxfendy is exciting and clinically meaningful for clinicians and patients. Epidemiological data indicate that a 10 mmHg decrease in systolic blood pressure is associated with a roughly 20% lower risk of serious cardiovascular events.”.

Industry observers note that aldosterone regulates sodium and water balance in the body. Excessive levels cause the kidneys to retain fluid, increasing blood pressure and potentially contributing to kidney inflammation and scarring.

Baxdrostat inhibits the enzyme responsible for producing aldosterone rather than blocking the hormone’s receptors, as some existing medications do. This approach may benefit patients whose blood pressure remains high despite multiple treatments.

A separate Phase 3 trial, Bax24, involving 218 patients found that baxdrostat lowered average systolic blood pressure over 24 hours by 14.0 mm Hg more than placebo. The effect persisted throughout the day and night, according to findings published in The Lancet.

Sources indicate that high blood pressure and chronic kidney disease can worsen each other. Elevated pressure damages the kidneys’ filtering structures, while declining kidney function makes hypertension harder to control.

“These findings are encouraging for people living with chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure, two conditions that often go hand-in-hand and create a dangerous cycle,” noted lead study author Jamie P. Dwyer, M.D., a professor of medicine at University of Utah Health. “High blood pressure can worsen kidney function and declining kidney function can further elevate blood pressure, and these outcomes can be life-altering for patients.”.

In the Phase 2 FigHTN trial, 192 patients with chronic kidney disease and uncontrolled hypertension were randomly assigned to receive baxdrostat or placebo alongside standard treatment. After 26 weeks, systolic blood pressure fell an average of 8.1 mm Hg more in the baxdrostat groups.

Researchers also measured urinary albumin, a protein associated with kidney damage when present in elevated amounts. Levels were 55% lower in patients receiving baxdrostat than in those taking placebo. The findings were published in the Journal of the American Society of Nephrology.

According to recent reports, the earlier kidney disease trial found elevated blood potassium in 41% of baxdrostat recipients, compared with 5% of placebo recipients. Most cases were mild or moderate, but excessive potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythm disturbances. Serious adverse events occurred in 9% and 3% of participants, respectively.

Although subsequent Phase 3 hypertension studies reported no unexpected safety findings, potassium levels and kidney function require monitoring during treatment.

“The reduction in urine albumin gives us hope that baxdrostat may also help delay kidney damage. This potential is now being tested in two large Phase 3 trials to determine if baxdrostat delays the progression of kidney disease,” noted Dwyer.

Industry observers note that larger studies are investigating whether baxdrostat can preserve kidney function over time, including trials combining it with dapagliflozin, an established kidney-protective medication. Its FDA approval presently covers hypertension, not the prevention of kidney disease progression.

“These new findings are reassuring that this new class of antihypertensive medications are likely to have both kidney- and cardio-protective benefits and to be safe and effective for broad patient populations,” said Jordana B. Cohen, M.D., M.S.C.E., immediate past chair of the American Heart Association’s Hypertension and Kidney Cardiovascular Science Committee. “Patients with chronic kidney disease were historically often excluded from drug studies. It is particularly reassuring to know that patients with chronic kidney disease, who have very high rates of hypertension and elevated renin-angiotensin aldosterone activity, were represented in their own study, tolerated the medication well, and had both blood pressure and albuminuric benefits. This medication class could be a game changer in the management of hypertension in this patient group.”.

“Efficacy and Safety of Baxdrostat in Participants with CKD and Uncontrolled Hypertension: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial” by Jamie P. Dwyer, Noha Maklad, Ola Vedin, John Monyak, Robin Myte, Glenn M. Chertow, Hiddo J.L. Heerspink and Dustin J. Little, 6 September 2025, Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. DOI: 10.1681/ASN.0000000849.

At the Races: After the deluge

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.
  • Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.
  • “After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one newly introduced Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow stated in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one newly introduced Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow stated in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

According to recent reports, “Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she remarked. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”.

In a recent development, the ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two latest female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

Industry observers note that “We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming upcoming members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

Recent findings suggest that house Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she mentioned.

Sources indicate that blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

According to recent reports, not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

It has been revealed that taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after Latest York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Sources indicate that member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

According to recent reports, the firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

It has been revealed that D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he aims to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he remarked.

Sources indicate that keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

It has been revealed that not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

It has been revealed that blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance noted in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”.

Recent findings suggest that but the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”.

Industry observers note that staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle claims he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

In a recent development, bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

Industry observers note that A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

In a recent development, bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

According to recent reports, roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

Industry observers note that as Maine goes: The Fresh York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”.

Sources indicate that “These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ stated the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top problem: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”.

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are presently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

According to recent reports, in large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#54258. Mysterious Radio Signals From 5,000 Light-Years Away Lead Scientists to a Surprising Discovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (826 w)

Mysterious Radio Signals From 5,000 Light-Years Away Lead Scientists to a Surprising Discovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.
  • Mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours.
  • Industry observers note that now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an crucial clue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.

Mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours. Astronomers have found only about a dozen of these unusual sources, and one question has been especially difficult to answer: What is actually producing the pulses?

Industry observers note that now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an crucial clue. Known as GPM J071507−114153, it contains a white dwarf, the dense core left behind after a star dies, orbiting a companion remarkably similar to our Sun. The white dwarf spins once every eight minutes.

The discovery is unusual because astronomers have never before detected these radio pulses from a white dwarf paired with a Sun-like star. Previously identified systems producing similar signals have typically involved much smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs.

It has been revealed that these mysterious sources belong to a class called long-period transients (LPTs). Since researchers at the International Center for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) first discovered one in 2021, around a dozen have been identified. Several contain a white dwarf and another star, although astronomers have struggled to determine which one produces the radio signals.

In a recent development, scientists at the Curtin University node at the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun. Credit: Natasha Hurley-Walker.

In the newly discovered system, scientists finally had enough information to narrow down the source.

“This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” said Dr Sam McSweeney, the study’s lead author and a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory.

In a recent development, mcSweeney made the discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. To confirm and better understand the white dwarf’s movement, the team processed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Center.

Sources indicate that the radio pulses also revealed something unexpected about the white dwarf’s companion. Researchers detected evidence of stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to the activity associated with auroras here on Earth.

“As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.”.

The observation suggests astronomers can use radio signals to investigate magnetic activity on distant stars, even when those stars are thousands of light-years away.

“It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.”.

Both observations were described by Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, a co-author of the paper.

Industry observers note that finding such a rare system required several powerful telescopes working together. The researchers first identified its radio signals during a large survey of the Milky Way, then used additional observations to pinpoint its location.

“We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” mentioned Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

Once the radio source had been located, optical observations from the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star, the same broad class as our Sun.

Sources indicate that the MWA, led by Curtin University, is located at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia. MeerKAT, meanwhile, was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa’s North Cape province.

Both facilities are precursors to the larger SKA telescopes now being developed, SKA-Low in Australia and SKA-Mid in South Africa. These future observatories are expected to provide more detailed observations of unusual radio sources and help astronomers identify additional systems that have so far escaped detection.

“If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built,” stated Dr McSweeney.

Reference: “A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion” by Samuel J. McSweeney, Natasha Hurley-Walker, Arash Bahramian, Csanád Horváth, Nanda Rea, Antonio C. Rodriguez and Ingrid Pelisoli, 12 November 2026, Nature Astronomy. DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-03016-z.
