#54225. Latest Update: The Pentagon Is Planning for Blackouts That Last for Months. One Problem Could Doom the Strategy.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1161 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The Pentagon Is Planning for Blackouts That Last for Months. One Problem Could Doom the Strategy.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture a military base on day thirty of a regional blackout.
  • In a recent development, the Pentagon wants bases to keep working through outages like this.
  • Paul Stockton, a former assistant secretary of defense for homeland defense and Americas’ security affairs, tells Popular Mechanics that many defense installations “depend on civilian-operated water utilities that lie outside installation fencelines.” Suppose the base keeps its power on for three months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture a military base on day thirty of a regional blackout. Its generators are still going strong, but the local utility has stopped pumping water to the base. Keeping the lights on won’t do much good if there’s no water to cool computers or fight a fire.

In a recent development, the Pentagon wants bases to keep working through outages like this. In September, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced FORTRESS America, a strategy to help military bases withstand attacks and disruptions to civilian services. The goal was to keep essential operations going for at least three months without outside help. Pentagon installations official Dale Marks shared more details in October, explaining that power targets would range from 30 to 90 days, depending on the base, and critical supplies would need to be stocked for at least three months.

Paul Stockton, a former assistant secretary of defense for homeland defense and Americas’ security affairs, tells Popular Mechanics that many defense installations “depend on civilian-operated water utilities that lie outside installation fencelines.” Suppose the base keeps its power on for three months. Can it still do its job if the services outside the gate stop working?

The first thing to fail may be the water.

Stockton puts water at the top of his concerns. Beyond drinking supplies, bases need it for fire suppression and computer cooling, uses he calls “absolutely vital for mission execution at most bases.” Sanitation depends on water, too. “Losing that electricity-dependent water utility support would have devastating effects in an extended conflict,” he says. Even if the base’s generators are running perfectly, that won’t matter if there’s a fire and there’s no water running through the hydrants.

Some missions need very little from the outside world. Stockton notes bases that launch nuclear strikes with bombers or other nuclear forces depend relatively little on civilian services. Bases that send troops overseas are different. For them, keeping the base running is only the first step.

According to recent reports, A unit heading to a conflict in the Taiwan Strait could start its trip at a base hundreds of miles from the coast. Getting troops and equipment to a ship would mean relying on civilian transportation and a working seaport, Stockton states. Keeping a base running through a blackout would be an achievement. But if its troops and equipment can’t get to the fight, the military still has a problem.

A reactor could help with the fuel trucks.

In a recent development, keeping generators supplied creates another outside dependency. Stockton notes bases commonly run on natural gas or diesel, and an extended outage could disrupt deliveries. Bases may have room to store substantial diesel reserves, but replenishing them through a region with disabled infrastructure would be difficult.

Small nuclear reactors could help. A microreactor could power a base for a long time without regular fuel deliveries. In August, the Army said it would spend up to $2.2 billion on five companies to build reactors at five bases. It hopes to have the first one running by September 2028. Reactors won’t be the only answer, though. Marks has said bases will also use other energy sources, and the mix will vary by location.

Sources indicate that “You park the reactor, turn it on, and it just sits there being hot,” claims Brendan Kochunas, an associate professor of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences at the University of Michigan. Once engineers can get it running reliably, a base could go a long time without a fresh delivery of reactor fuel. Diesel generators, by contrast, would keep burning through their fuel supply.

The military microreactors are “very much still in development,” Kochunas says. Antares Nuclear, the manufacturer the Army chose to build a reactor at Fort Bragg, demonstrated a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in its Mark-0 reactor in June. Its follow-on Mark-1 is scheduled to demonstrate electricity production in 2027, according to the company’s congressional testimony.

Recent findings suggest that that leaves a big question: can a reactor keep going on its own? Kochunas indicates the real test comes when a reactor runs at full power for a long stretch. That’s when engineers find out what needs fixing, “once you see everything heat up.” A single broken pump or sensor could leave a base waiting for outside help. That’s the same kind of help a blackout could cut off. For Kochunas, a reactor is only ready when it has shown it can run “without interaction, only observation, for the duration of the anticipated mission outage.”.

The exercise has to follow the mission.

In a recent development, stockton claims the first step in knowing whether a base could really survive a blackout is a surprise test called a blackstart exercise. Without warning, the base cuts itself off from the grid and starts its own generators. Then it has to get power to the equipment its mission depends on. That’s harder than it sounds. “Such blackstart operations are challenging,” Stockton says. But a successful start only answers the first question—the next is how long the base can continue operating if fuel deliveries become unreliable or the water utility fails. An exercise that assumes those services will keep working could give commanders too much confidence in what the generators have accomplished.

Recent findings suggest that david Alexander, an emeritus professor of emergency planning and management at University College London, sees a similar matter in hospitals. They “function as part of the medical system. Hence, they do not work independently,” he states. Backup power keeps the building running, but it can’t replace everything else a hospital depends on to do its job.

The strongest fortress may extend beyond the fence.

Sources indicate that so where should the money go? Stockton indicates one of the best investments might not be on the base at all. The pumps that send water to the base sit at the local water utility. So if a blackout shuts them down, the base’s taps and hydrants will go dry. Helping the utility keep its own power on could do more for the mission than spending on the base itself. Stockton also wants planners to think bigger than one base and its town. In a 2026 report for the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, he proposed choosing large sections of the grid, some covering several states, that could cut themselves off when trouble started spreading elsewhere. He calls them “microgrids on steroids.”.

First, utilities would need a proposal to keep the power on inside each section. If that works, a region’s seaports could keep running along with its bases, and troops and equipment would have a real chance of reaching their ships. Hegseth has promised that if an adversary takes down the grid, “our bases stay lit.” That’s an notable goal, but just keeping the lights on isn’t enough. The real goal is getting troops to where the fight is—and a base that can’t do that is just a well-lit place to wait.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

In a recent development, children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, indicates archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

In a recent development, this evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

According to recent reports, the purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Sources indicate that davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”.

Industry observers note that departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

Recent findings suggest that “I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries remarked on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

According to recent reports, departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

Industry observers note that it’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for fresh members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

In a recent development, “I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island mentioned in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build significant things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of fresh well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

It has been revealed that "We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the upcoming Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., remarked in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy stated in a Friday statement.

Industry News: Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
  • On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Sources indicate that didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”.

Sources indicate that DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.).

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so promptly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Sources indicate that scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” notes planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Industry observers note that juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

It has been revealed that “Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” states planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer upcoming avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

Recent findings suggest that for example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” states planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

In a recent development, similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer.
  • After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.
  • Industry observers note that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

Industry observers note that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned on Monday evening.

It has been revealed that asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

In a recent development, though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

It has been revealed that “Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I stated, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Industry observers note that johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

In a recent development, also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

According to recent reports, “We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he mentioned, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

In a recent development, but Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, mentioned she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the aims and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

It has been revealed that that includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

It has been revealed that republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott mentioned. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

Recent findings suggest that “A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick mentioned in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly mentioned Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

Breaking: The fight to save one of Australia’s rarest frogs has taken a cue from farmers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Selective breeding could help Australia’s southern corroboree frog survive longer after exposure to the deadly chytrid fungus.
  • A breeding technique from agriculture might help one of Australia’s most threatened frogs.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers found that southern corroboree frogs can inherit traits that help them survive longer after exposure to a deadly fungus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Selective breeding could help Australia’s southern corroboree frog survive longer after exposure to the deadly chytrid fungus.

A breeding technique from agriculture might help one of Australia’s most threatened frogs.

Recent findings suggest that researchers found that southern corroboree frogs can inherit traits that help them survive longer after exposure to a deadly fungus. That means selective breeding could make the species more resilient.

According to recent reports, the frog is functionally extinct in the wild. The culprit is chytridiomycosis, an infectious disease caused by the amphibian chytrid fungus.

In a recent development, captive breeding has kept the species alive. But returning frogs to the wild is hard because the fungus persists in the environment.

Lead author Mikaeylah Davidson completed the work as part of her PhD at the University of Melbourne.

The study tested whether genomic selection could guide conservation breeding for the frog.

In a recent development, davidson and her colleagues combined laboratory experiments with genome-wide genetic information. That included a custom genotyping array built for the frog.

In a recent development, the team found that southern corroboree frogs differ in how long they survive after exposure to chytrid fungus. Some of that variation is inherited.

“Using genomic data, we were able to show that survival following chytrid infection is a heritable trait, meaning some of the differences in survival are due to genetic differences that can be passed on to the next generation,” Davidson said.

“This means there is genetic variation we could potentially use to improve survival through selective breeding.”.

“Excitingly, this approach is a potential way to move beyond simply keeping endangered frogs alive in captivity, towards actively improving their ability to cope with the threats preventing their recovery in the wild.”.

Modeling suggested genomic information could guide breeding decisions.

It could potentially increase average survival time after exposure to chytrid fungus by around nine percent in the next generation.

The model projected that gain while accounting for inbreeding and genetic diversity.

An established captive breeding program offered a chance to test the idea in practice. Zoos Victoria and the Taronga Conservation Society support that program through partnerships.

In a recent development, the research suggests improved disease resilience doesn’t need to come at the expense of genetic diversity. That is especially significant for small, critically endangered populations.

In such groups, maintaining diversity and limiting inbreeding are central to long-term population health and evolutionary potential.

Senior author Lee Skerratt from the University of Melbourne argued the approach may also have potential for other threatened wildlife affected by persistent disease.

That is particularly true for species already managed through captive breeding.

“Amphibians are an important focus, with hundreds of species now maintained in captivity for conservation as chytrid fungus continues to threaten populations globally,” he said.

“Genomic selection could help conservation breeding programs move beyond preventing extinction by moving animals into captivity towards actively supporting animals’ ability to survive threats in the wild.”.

This work builds on six years of effort.

In a recent development, first, researchers developed the genomic tools and disease datasets needed to explore new strategies for the frog. They then combined a newly mapped genome and a custom genotyping array with extensive disease-resilience data.

That let them investigate selective breeding as a proactive approach to species recovery.

The next stage is to improve and validate the predictions.

Industry observers note that the team will use genomic information from more of the breeding population. They will also explore other genetic approaches to improve disease resistance.

In a recent development, researchers will also test whether the predicted improvements show up in later generations. And critically, they will check whether greater survival in the lab translates into better outcomes in the wild.

Amphibians are in deep trouble worldwide. The chytrid fungus has caused catastrophic declines and extinctions.

More than 200 threatened frog species are now kept in captivity. These colonies have prevented immediate extinctions.

But they are temporary refuges, meant to hold the line until threats can be mitigated.

Selective breeding offers a different path. Instead of just keeping animals alive, it can improve their ability to cope. That could raise the odds of successful reintroduction.

Industry observers note that while genomic selection has transformed plant and animal breeding, it has rarely been applied to wildlife. The main barriers have been missing datasets and a lack of structured breeding programs.

This frog had both, which made it an ideal test case.

The species produces fewer than 30 eggs per year and reaches sexual maturity at 2 to 5 years of age. Those traits slow generational turnover.

According to recent reports, the trait is also polygenic. No single gene has a large effect. Resistance is shaped by many loci, each contributing a little.

Because many genes contribute to survival, the team used genomic selection, which draws on information from across the genome.

And the modelling covers only part of the breeding population. Future work could capture more genetic variation.

The team proposes a phased rollout.

According to recent reports, first, refine the breeding value predictions with more parental genotyping. Second, test realized responses in controlled and semi-natural conditions. Third, run multi-generational selective breeding alongside ongoing diversity management.

In a recent development, data from each phase would feed back into the program. That supports adaptive management and continuous improvement.

According to recent reports, for now, the result is a proof of concept. It shows that captive populations can become more than passive safeguards. For a frog on the brink, that shift could matter a great deal.

The study is published in the journal npj Biodiversity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
  • In a recent development, neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

In a recent development, neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

In a recent development, the study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, indicates neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

Sources indicate that “You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman notes. The newly introduced study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao claims.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are right now no broadly effective treatments.

Industry observers note that the hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao states. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao claims.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

Laser printers, known for printing crisp, professional-looking documents swiftly, are generally considered big, expensive machines designed for large offices. While some larger models live up to that reputation, plenty of compact options fit into your home office if you print files often.

It has been revealed that while more expensive than an inkjet printer, most laser printers are a better long-term investment, with lower operating costs and designs built for heavy-duty printing. That noted, choosing the right one at a glance can be tricky, and may vary based on your needs.

Industry observers note that printers aren’t the most exciting tech products, and many folks see them as frustrating, unreliable machines that require constant repair or replacement and are increasingly unnecessary for the average person in the digital age. While that may be true for some, they remain essential for workers who need to print contracts or create physical records, and students who need hard copies of their homework. With a little research, you can find a good laser printer that makes life easier and lasts a long time.

The recommended printers are based on my personal experience and knowledge of printers, as well as research from reputable publications, including PCMag and The Wirecutter. I looked for printers with performance and features that suit both home and small office users, with price and value in mind. I also spent months testing the best overall pick and using it as my everyday printer to ensure it’s a worthy recommendation.

I have been reviewing tech products for 25 years, including computing peripherals such as inkjet and laser printers. As an editor at Computer Shopper magazine, I helped develop the printer testing methodology used in the reviews. I then brought that expertise to publications such as Digital Trends and Business Insider, applying real-world usage that resonates with shoppers in the evaluation.

There’s no perfect laser printer, but if you’re looking for a reliable, easy-to-use unit that produces high-quality prints, the HP LaserJet Pro MFP 3101sdw fits the bill. I’ve been using this printer for several months and found that it’s an ideal fit for my home office. It also has plenty of advanced features that would make it a good fit for a small business.

With a 35ppm print speed, the 3101sdw is fast for its intended audience. When connected to a typical home Wi-Fi network, it takes about 5 seconds from pressing print to outputting the first page. Printed text looks good even at lower-quality settings, with small fonts staying sharp and legible. I found the scan quality more than adequate for everyday use, but 300 dpi is too low for designers, photographers, and other creative users. It also runs quiet, which is always a nice bonus.

It has been revealed that anybody who needs to make copies will find the ADF-equipped scanner handy, while the 2.7-inch touchscreen makes setup easy. It took me less than 10 minutes to get it up and running. Whether you connect via USB, Ethernet, or Wi-Fi, the printer responds swiftly. It also has a USB port for quick prints or saving scans to a flash drive.

While the 3101sdw is small enough to fit on a large desk, it’s more practical to put it on its own stand. I wouldn’t call it “lightweight,” but I could carry it down five floors without much effort. It won’t win any design awards, either, which is too bad because HP generally knows how to make great-looking products.

Recent findings suggest that the paper tray has an average 250-page capacity, but a notable drawback is that it has no manual feed tray. I didn’t find this an concern, but if you need to, say, print on envelopes, it could be problematic because you'd have to switch out the paper in the main tray. Another expert reviewer dinged the 3101sdw for lacking a fax function, but my workaround is to use the HP Smart companion app to scan and send (but not receive) faxes.

The 3101sdw offers stronger print quality, a better build, and ease of use. It’s hard to say how long mechanical devices like this will last, but HP’s printers are known for their reliability—I have a LaserJet from the 1990s that’s still going strong.

In a recent development, in my experience, Brother makes affordable laser printers that consistently deliver solid performance and text quality. At 36ppm and under $200, the HL-L2460DW is a strong basic option for a home or small office. Despite its barebones design, it has useful features like double-sided printing, Ethernet connectivity, wireless printing, a generous 250-page paper capacity, and a mobile app. Plus, it’s lightweight and doesn’t take up too much space.

Industry observers note that the HL-L2460DW supports a 1,200-page standard-yield toner cartridge or 3,000-page high-yield toner cartridge, but comes with a starter cartridge that only yields 700 pages out of the box. (This is typical of printer manufacturers.) If you plan to print a lot, I’d recommend buying a high-yield cartridge right when you buy the printer.

This is a “budget” option, though, so this printer comes with a few caveats. I don’t love the small LCD display, which has a basic interface that doesn’t display much info and doesn’t feel as well-made. The basic operation means there’s no scanning, copying, faxing, ADF, or other multi-function capabilities. Plus, black-and-white graphics and images don’t look as good as text. User reviews have also complained about its reliability. Still, given its balance of price, speed, and print quality, the HL-L2460DW is a good value regardless of budget.

If it’s for personal use and you only blueprint to use it every so often, I’d steer you toward a different model, the HL-L2420DW, which has a 30ppm speed and every aforementioned feature except Ethernet. It’s perfect for casual printing, and it costs $50 less.

Sources indicate that most offices shy away from color laser printers because they are expensive to buy and maintain, and employees often use them to make wasteful prints. Likewise, at home, you’re probably better off going with a color inkjet printer. That remarked, if you truly need color prints, I love the HP Color LaserJet Pro MFP 3301fdw, which delivers excellent print quality and attractive features like glossy paper support. It’s a strong, if pricey, complement to any office.

Despite its compact footprint, the 3301fdw has a 50-page duplexing ADF and a 250-page paper tray. It’s not the fastest color laser printer, but its 26ppm speed is more than adequate for home or small business use.

In a recent development, print quality is where HP’s laser printers excel. You can expect documents with crisp text and well-saturated, natural-looking color graphics and photos. Unlike most laser printers, the 3301fdw is compatible with select HP glossy paper, so you can make photo prints. They don’t really compare to inkjet photo printers, but it’s fine in most cases.

Sources indicate that like our overall pick, the 3301fdw is a breeze to set up via its 4.3-inch color touchscreen. For connectivity, it supports USB, Ethernet, and Wi-Fi, which covers most home and office networks.

Sources indicate that you may have guessed the printer’s substantial con is that it’s pricey to operate. Whether you’re using the standard or high-yield toner options, the cost per page is high. If you’re looking to spend a little less, I’d look at the Brother MFC-L3380CDW, which has a comparable feature set to the 3301fdw and a lower operating cost. You’re compromising a bit on print quality and performance, though, which is why the HP leads the pack.

A true small-business laser printer needs to be a workhorse. It should offer a robust, office-centric range of features, print fast, support multiple owners, hold enough paper, and have a high duty cycle. Experts agree that Brother makes some of the best laser printers for offices, and the monochrome MFC-L2900DW multi-function model is a particularly good option.

Imagine the L2900DW as an enhanced version of the HL-L2460DW. It shares a similar design, small footprint, and print engine, but features a high-capacity 50-page ADF for copying or scanning multi-page documents. The L2900DW also has a single-page duplexing scanner for two-sided pages. There’s even a fax function.

A large 3.5-inch touchscreen makes setup and on-device operation easy without a computer, while USB, Wi-Fi, and Ethernet give you options for connecting. Combined with a fast 36ppm speed, sharp text print quality, low operating cost, and the option to use high-yield cartridges, you’ve got a very capable all-in-one laser printer.

It has been revealed that graphics don’t look as sharp as text, but that shouldn’t matter if your office prints mainly documents. While its 250-page paper tray is adequate for a small business, expect to reload often if multiple customers print often. This model offers no option for a larger or expandable paper tray.

In a recent development, the ADF has a scanner resolution of just 600 dpi, but that is plenty for text documents; the flatbed scanner has 1,200 dpi, which is fine for color images. The output tray’s 100-page capacity is low for heavy usage. One missing feature is a front USB port, which is handy for printing or faxing documents from a flash drive or saving scans to one.

If you need to support a large number of workers, consider stepping up to Brother’s MFC-L5915DW. It has a 70-page ADF and a 5-inch LCD, and you can expand its paper capacity beyond the standard 250 pages. With a faster 50ppm speed, support for 18,000-page high-yield cartridges, and a higher duty cycle, it’s an ideal choice for busy offices. It’s a big jump in price, which is why I went with the L2900DW, but it may cost less to operate in the long run.

According to recent reports, whether for the office or your home, a laser printer is a good option if you often print many multi-page documents. If you need a home printer for occasional printing, a more affordable inkjet printer may make more sense. Again, a laser printer costs more up front but pays dividends in the long run as a professional tool or a home tech staple. If you’re on the fence about what to buy, here are the things I look at when I evaluate laser printers:.

In a recent development, most prints from a laser printer are black-and-white text documents, and most models deliver decent print quality. If you need to print impactful pages with photos and charts, a color laser printer can print higher-quality graphics. Even the best monochrome printers we’ve tested and researched can’t match the detail and clarity of color ink toner. For example, if you have a multi-colored pie chart, a monochrome reproduction can only do so much to separate the different color shading.

Keep in mind, though, that even the cheapest color laser printer will be expensive, and its print quality may not rival that of higher-end models. They also do not support specialty media like glossy photo paper.

In a recent development, A basic laser printer’s sole function is to print documents, and that’s enough for most people. It’s generally compact and fits on a desk. But if you run a small business or work remotely in a home office, you may want a multi-function, “all-in-one” printer that scans and copies, too, among other tasks. Multi-function printers are far more useful, but they’re larger and cost more due to the extra hardware inside.

Recent findings suggest that “Yield” refers to the estimated number of pages you can get out of a single toner cartridge. Most laser printers should get around 1,500 pages from a toner cartridge, while high-yield cartridges should last 3,000 pages or more.

Toner cartridges are expensive, especially for color printers, but they offer a better cost per page than ink. My rule of thumb is that high-yield toners will save you money in the long run.

According to recent reports, similarly, a laser printer’s “duty cycle” rating refers to the maximum number of prints per month that the manufacturer recommends to keep it in proper working order. Basic laser printers have a duty cycle of around 5,000 pages or less, while heavy-duty models have ratings of 10,000 or higher. Printing beyond the rated duty cycle can lead to breakdowns, more maintenance, or a shorter lifespan.

For personal use or small businesses that print occasionally, 25 to 30 pages per minute (ppm) should be fine. Small offices with a few employees that print often may want a faster printer with a speed of 35 to 40 ppm. In a larger office, I’d look for at least 40 ppm, if not more. Keep in mind that manufacturers measure speeds under ideal conditions, and real-world results may not always match. Expect a small discrepancy of a few pages.

Recent findings suggest that most printers rely primarily on a USB cable to connect to your computer, but a hard-wired connection alone isn’t practical in today’s world of wireless laptops, phones, and tablets. I recommend choosing a printer with a wireless connection compatible with your most-used devices, such as Wi-Fi or Apple AirPrint. Some laser printers also support Ethernet for a high-speed hard-wired connection. Office-focused machines may include a front USB port so you can plug in a flash drive with the files you need to print.

According to recent reports, most laser printers have a paper tray that holds 250 pages, which is enough for personal and small business use. Some compact printers may have a smaller capacity–around 150 pages. If you expect to print a lot, consider a model with a higher-capacity tray or support for multiple trays, and look for an output tray large enough to hold everything you print out. All printers also have a multi-purpose tray for manually feeding non-standard paper like envelopes.

In addition to the essentials, there are some features that I look for which are nice to have, but won’t make or break a printer:.

Depending on the model, it can be basic or advanced. Depending on your use case, you may consider some or all of these essential. That remarked, they aren't universal, and some printers work well without them.

Laser printers use toner, a powder heated onto paper, while inkjet printers spray ink droplets. Laser printers are considered superior for their speed and print quality, but they are expensive to purchase and maintain. Inkjet printers offer color printing and affordability, but prints need time to dry, and the cost per page can be higher with heavy use.

However, the best modern inkjet printers today are fast and deliver great-looking prints, especially photos. They also support different paper types and sizes. Laser printers can also print in color, but they're pricey. Beyond speed, their advantages include consistent print quality and long-term reliability.

Sources indicate that which technology is better ultimately depends on your needs. Most people will find an inkjet printer sufficient and more versatile, but those who print often may find a laser printer more economical in the long run. In an ideal setup, consider an affordable laser printer for frequent print jobs and a good inkjet printer for color documents and photos.

In a recent development, color laser printers can print photos and graphics on standard paper, but if you want to print on photo paper, an inkjet is the better choice, especially one that supports multi-color ink tanks. Laser printers aren’t designed for photo-quality reproduction, and generally don’t work with specialty paper. (As we discussed, some HP models are compatible with select glossy paper.).

In a recent development, depending on usage and maintenance, a laser printer can last for many years. It’s a mechanical device, though, so there’s no guarantee that it won’t break down and require service. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

In a recent development, “We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” remarked a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

In a recent development, republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Fresh Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

  • It has been revealed that more than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit.
  • It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that more than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

According to recent reports, these fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston claims. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”.

According to recent reports, angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston notes.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”.

Tech Report: The power grid’s toughest hour of the year may no longer come on a summer afternoon

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Heat pumps could reshape the power grid more than climate change, pushing the worst demand spikes in cold regions into winter by 2060.
  • Ask when the power grid has its hardest day and most people picture a heat wave, with every air conditioner in town running at once.
  • Across much of the northern United States, that day may soon be a cold winter night instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heat pumps could reshape the power grid more than climate change, pushing the worst demand spikes in cold regions into winter by 2060.

Ask when the power grid has its hardest day and most people picture a heat wave, with every air conditioner in town running at once.

Across much of the northern United States, that day may soon be a cold winter night instead.

Upcoming modeling finds that as homes swap gas furnaces for heat pumps, the worst spikes in electricity demand in cold regions could grow by half to nearly double by 2060.

With today’s heating and cooling equipment, warming alone changes extreme peaks by less than 10% in either direction.

The model projects much larger increases in cold regions as buildings switch to electric heating.

Mai Shi, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Michigan‘s School for Environment and Sustainability, led the work with colleagues at Michigan, MIT and Cornell University.

Sources indicate that their projections cover 183 counties through 2060 and hold the number of buildings fixed. Every change they report comes from weather and equipment, not from newly introduced construction or population growth.

“We focused on the extreme peak demands because we want to keep our power systems reliable,” Shi remarked.

According to recent reports, “If the system works for moderate conditions but fails in extremes, it doesn’t work. That’s not how we build the power grid. We need to blueprint for extremes.”.

An electric heat pump can both heat and cool a building. When it replaces a gas furnace, heating shifts onto the power grid. The standard heat pump in the study lost heating capacity as outdoor temperatures fell.

The standard unit in the study keeps only half of its rated heating capacity at 5°F (-15°C).

In the team’s model, heat pumps and insulation spread through buildings at the pace home air conditioning spread across the country, about 10% a year.

With that pace of adoption and today’s weather, the most extreme peaks grow by 60% to 104% by 2060 across the six cold regions.

In a recent development, those are New England, New York, the Midwest, the Mid-Atlantic, the Northwest and the Great Plains. The season changes too.

At the start of the projections, more than 95% of those regions’ yearly peaks fall in summer.

By 2060, more than 95% fall in winter. Insulation lowers demand, but in cold regions it can’t cancel out the furnaces being replaced.

Run the same buildings through a warming climate with today’s equipment and the changes are smaller.

Extreme peaks rise 3% to 9% in every region but the Northwest, as extreme heat pushes up cooling demand. In the Northwest, winter heating already sets the peak, and a milder winter trims it by 3%.

Put the two drivers together and they don’t simply add up. Warmer winters offset part of the heat pump demand, cutting the growth in cold-region extremes by up to 18% compared with technology alone.

Industry observers note that the net result in those regions is still a 48% to 93% increase through 2060. That is up to roughly 10 times what warming alone would do. Warming also delays the switch to winter peaking rather than stopping it.

Researchers call the spread of a technology through homes tech diffusion.

“Tech diffusion may have a larger impact than climate change on peak demand in a lot of regions,” remarked Shi, who is also a member of the university’s Center for Sustainable Systems.

It has been revealed that in the projections for California and Texas, the peak stays in summer. Heat pumps and insulation make cooling more efficient there, so the technology lowers extreme peaks instead of raising them.

With warming included, those two regions’ extremes end up 1% to 9% lower than they would be under climate change alone.

Industry observers note that the Southwest and Southeast are in between. Technology alone pushes their extremes up 17% and 11%, because about 60% of their yearly peaks move to winter while the rest stay in summer.

According to recent reports, A winter peak on a cold night can run higher than a summer one. Warming lowers those winter extremes by 4% to 6%.

In Texas, faster adoption lowers the peak further. Under climate change alone, the largest peak between 2020 and 2060 is 12% above today’s.

With the fastest spread of heat pumps and insulation, that increase shrinks to 5%.

The team trained 209,352 machine learning models on simulated hourly heating and cooling use for 362,227 homes and commercial buildings across 183 counties.

The counties were chosen so that each state’s mix of weather zones matched the real one.

The researchers used 100 simulations from four climate models and three emissions scenarios to project how future weather could affect electricity demand for heating and cooling.

In a recent development, adoption speed came from history. The researchers looked at how fast 18 past technologies spread, from vacuum cleaners at about 2% a year to cell phones at about 36%. Home air conditioning, at 10%, was their main case.

In a recent development, the researchers used the 95th percentile of projected annual peaks to estimate extreme demand. Only about one in 20 of those peaks exceeds that level.

Industry observers note that in the projections, peaks change little through the early 2030s and the weather is nearly the whole source of uncertainty. In cold regions, that changes in the late 2030s and the 2040s.

Sources indicate that heat pump adoption reaches the steep part of its curve and winter peaks grow quickly. From one climate run to the next, it becomes uncertain whether a year’s peak falls in summer or winter.

Recent findings suggest that the spread of possible peaks in those regions widens to three or four times its 2020 level by the 2050s. By then, winter peaking is established in most of them.

In a recent development, for grid planners, the source of uncertainty moves with that transition. By the 2050s, how fast people adopt the technology is the largest single factor in New England and New York, at 65% to 75% of the total.

Climate still drives 85% to 99% in the Southeast, the Northwest and California.

Michael Craig is the study’s senior author and an associate professor at Michigan.

“Climate change still matters a lot. If I’m thinking about my power system and what I should worry about, climate change is still an key source of risk and uncertainty,” Craig mentioned.

According to recent reports, the team also tested a heat pump that keeps 90% of its heating capacity at 5°F instead of 50%. With it, extreme peaks come out 5% to 40% lower, with the biggest savings in cold regions.

Sources indicate that the projections hold the equipment’s performance fixed over 40 years, so they don’t include heat pumps improving, or smart thermostats and thermal storage moving demand off the worst hours. They cover heating and cooling only.

Electric vehicle charging isn’t in them, and neither are data centers.

One recent tally of utility forecasts attributes roughly half of the projected growth in U.S. peak load through 2030 to data centers.

Humidity isn’t in the model either, only temperature. And it assumes heat pumps spread at the same pace everywhere, when energy prices, housing and policy will set different speeds in different states.

In a recent development, how fast adoption will actually run in each region is the open question. Shi said that number, unlike the weather, is one that local rules and incentives can steer.

The authors wrote that the next step is building those regional differences into the projections, so that each region’s planners see the projection that applies to them.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
