#54182. Thanksgiving food waste can start before the turkey even goes in the oven

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1399 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Thanksgiving food waste can start before the turkey even goes in the oven

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans wasted about 166,000 metric tons of food during Thanksgiving week in 2025, roughly 39% more than during a comparison week.
  • When Thanksgiving food waste comes up, leftovers usually get the blame.
  • Sources indicate that the stuffing went unfinished, or half a pie stayed on the counter until Sunday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans wasted about 166,000 metric tons of food during Thanksgiving week in 2025, roughly 39% more than during a comparison week.

When Thanksgiving food waste comes up, leftovers usually get the blame.

Sources indicate that the stuffing went unfinished, or half a pie stayed on the counter until Sunday. In some homes, though, good food is discarded before the meal is even cooked. It is thrown out so a shelf can be cleared for the turkey.

Researchers documented this habit in surveys of U.S. households around Thanksgiving 2025. More edible food was discarded by those households in the holiday week than in a later, ordinary week.

Recent findings suggest that extra waste was reported by cooks who emptied the fridge to make room. Cooks who had to guess their guests’ appetites reported more too, compared with cooks who made just enough.

The researchers therefore see the days before the meal as a chance to cut holiday waste.

Ran Li of Penn State University and Brian Roe of Ohio State University carried out the surveys. Roe is a professor of agricultural, environmental and development economics.

According to recent reports, all of the figures are based on people’s own reports about their kitchens. Nobody’s trash was actually weighed.

“There’s not a lot of great data out there about which holidays cause the most waste,” Roe remarked. “My money would be on Thanksgiving because it is so focused around the meal – it is the massive tradition.”.

Household waste surveys normally skip holiday weeks, since researchers are after a typical week. Yearly totals based on such surveys therefore miss the holidays.

According to recent reports, for this study, 879 adults were surveyed before and after Thanksgiving 2025. Every one of them handled at least half of the cooking at home.

About a week after the first survey, they reported how much food their households had not eaten. That included anything thrown out, composted or fed to pets.

Bones, peels and pits were left out of the count. Only once-edible food was included.

Later, in December, 437 of the same households repeated the exercise for a non-holiday week.

Households that reported in both weeks discarded about 1.1 pounds (500 grams) of edible food per person during Thanksgiving week.

About 0.8 pounds (358 grams) was discarded in the December week. The Thanksgiving total was therefore 39% higher.

People who skipped the holiday meal discarded about the same amount in both weeks.

The results were then scaled up to the whole country. By the authors’ estimate, Americans discarded about 367 million pounds (166,000 metric tons) of edible food during Thanksgiving week.

That amounts to roughly a pound for every person in the United States.

Based on respondents’ estimates, Americans wasted about $3 billion worth of edible food during Thanksgiving week, roughly 40% more than during the December comparison week.

“That’s a pretty healthy chunk of change, particularly as people are concerned about high food prices right now,” Roe noted.

Four out of five respondents took part in a Thanksgiving meal as a host, a guest or both.

About 0.8 pounds (356 grams) per person was discarded that week by people who neither hosted nor attended a meal.

Guests who did not host averaged 1.2 pounds (545 grams). Hosts who did not attend another meal averaged 1.1 pounds (493 grams).

Industry observers note that the highest average, 1.8 pounds (818 grams), was reported by respondents who hosted one meal and attended another. That is more than double the amount for people who skipped the holiday.

These gaps remained after age, income, household size and shopping habits were taken into account.

According to recent reports, the meal was not blamed for all of that week’s waste. About a quarter of the discarded food was tied by respondents to hosting or attending a Thanksgiving meal.

Different foods were also thrown out by hosts and guests. More meat, turkey included, was discarded by hosts than by guests. Half of the people who only attended a meal had cooked a dish at home to bring.

About 500 respondents cooked for a Thanksgiving meal, either as hosts or as guests bringing a dish. Of those cooks, 74% said they had deliberately made more food than was needed.

Sources indicate that the cooks gave three main reasons. Leftovers were the goal for the largest group, 37% of the cooks. Another 25% did not know how much their guests would eat. A further 12% said a big spread was the tradition.

Each of these groups reported more waste than cooks who tried to make just enough. Leftover planners reported about 0.4 pounds (189 grams) more per person for the week.

Cooks who were unsure reported about 0.8 pounds (363 grams) more.

A plan for the extra food was thus associated with less waste than a guess was.

In a recent development, for cooks who guess, tools such as the Guest-Imator were suggested by Li and Roe. It is a calculator from the Natural Resources Defense Council.

A guest count and the amount of leftovers wanted are entered, and the calculator returns quantities to buy.

A use for the extra food was found by many cooks. Among hosts, 37% sent guests home with leftovers. About one in six respondents with leftovers froze some.

Sources indicate that the cooks were also asked about the days before the meal. Had food been thrown away to make room for the turkey and the other holiday groceries?

About one in five cooks said yes.

Nearly a pound (438 grams) more waste per person was reported for the week by cooks who cleared space. The comparison was with meal participants who neither cleared space nor cooked too much.

That extra amount alone exceeds the 0.8 pounds reported for the whole week by a person who skipped Thanksgiving.

“They would clear out a bunch of stuff,” Roe mentioned.

Li and Roe wrote that campaigns before the holiday could help. One example they gave was recipes that use up fridge items the night before the turkey is bought.

“Think about what’s in the fridge that can be used up before the turkey’s coming in so that you can have that place for all your fixings for the holiday meal,” he said.

Respondents also reported where the food went: the trash, the compost or the sink.

During Thanksgiving week, 98% more food per person went down the sink or garbage disposal than in December.

Residents of some cities are warned around the holidays about fatbergs. These are buildups of fat, oil and grease that can damage sewer pipes.

According to recent reports, the kind of food that went down the drain was not recorded. However, 85% more meat and fish was discarded during Thanksgiving week by households that reported in both weeks.

Li and Roe suspect that holiday cooking adds fat, oil and grease to what goes down the sink.

Sources indicate that because the study is a survey, it shows which habits were associated with more waste. It cannot show that any single habit caused the waste.

According to recent reports, the respondents were drawn from an online research panel. Their answers were adjusted to match U.S. households on age, income and household size. Even so, the respondents were not a random sample.

It has been revealed that in earlier research, surveys of this kind found 32% to 52% less waste than physical measurement of household waste did. The national totals may therefore be underestimates.

According to recent reports, each household’s waste was also divided by the number of people who normally live there. The number of people at the table was not used. A host’s figure therefore looks bigger, and a guest’s figure looks smaller.

Only about half of the Thanksgiving respondents reported again in December.

For some of them, the December week ended just before Christmas. That week may not have been an ordinary one either.

The survey also did not test any solution. It remains unknown if a portion calculator or a night of use-it-up cooking reduces what is thrown out.

According to Li and Roe, household waste should be weighed over a holiday in future studies.

They also recommended that similar surveys be run for other food-centered holidays.

The full study was published in the journal Waste.

#54179. Offshore wind turbines may reshape the low clouds around them

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1229 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Offshore wind turbines may reshape the low clouds around them

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1229 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clouds can change how much electricity offshore wind farms produce, while turbines can also thin low clouds nearby.
  • Recent findings suggest that low clouds over the sea do more than just block sunlight.
  • This moving air also affects the wind turbines below.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clouds can change how much electricity offshore wind farms produce, while turbines can also thin low clouds nearby.

Recent findings suggest that low clouds over the sea do more than just block sunlight. The tops of these clouds lose heat to space, which cools the air and keeps it moving.

This moving air also affects the wind turbines below.

In computer simulations, turbines in the last rows produced about 11% more power when the air above the clouds was drier than when it was moister.

Industry observers note that the wind turbines also affected the clouds. When the clouds were low enough to touch the turbine blades, the turbines made them thinner over several miles in the direction of the wind.

Clouds are left out of many simulations of offshore wind farms.

It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands put them in. Their results suggest that planners of large offshore farms should take clouds into account.

All of this was tested in computer simulations, not at real wind farms.

According to recent reports, the clouds in question are stratocumulus. These low, lumpy sheets are the most common cloud type on Earth.

Sources indicate that in an average year, they cover about 25% to 30% of the North Sea. Wind energy projects are widespread there, and more are planned.

Recent findings suggest that the North Sea is cloudy so often that its wind farms’ energy output may be affected, mentioned Davide Selvatici. Selvatici is a postdoctoral researcher in the university’s Physics of Fluids group.

Modelers had often worked with idealized skies that held almost no cloud, stated Richard Stevens. Stevens is a professor of fluid mechanics at Twente.

Sources indicate that thijs van den Ham, a co-author, mentioned wind farm simulations need clouds in them. “They do play a role, and they do matter,” the author added.

Humidity by itself doesn’t do much to a turbine. Moist air and dry air differ in density by less than 1%. Power output changes by about the same amount.

So the team looked at how clouds change the air’s motion. An earlier study by Selvatici and Stevens had already examined this. In that work, the slowed wind behind a simulated farm recovered faster under low clouds.

The simulations were detailed enough to follow individual gusts and swirls of air.

The work was done in two stages. Cloud layers were first simulated without any turbines, and the temperature and moisture of the overlying air were varied. About 300 simulated hours passed before each of those layers reached a steady state.

A wind farm was then added beneath a selection of those cloud layers. It had 60 turbines in 10 staggered rows, and each was rated at 10 megawatts.

Rotors measured 585 feet (178 meters) across, which put the blade tips 682 feet (208 meters) above the water.

The Washington Monument is shorter than that. At such a height, the blades could reach into the lowest simulated clouds.

Recent findings suggest that A block of air 37 miles (60 kilometers) long surrounded the farm in the model. The block was divided into more than 560 million cells.

Two sets of runs were carried out so that the cloud’s effect could be separated from the effect of moisture.

Cooling at the cloud top was held fixed in the first set. In the second set, cooling was allowed to respond to the moisture overhead, which is how real clouds behave.

When cooling was held fixed, the drier and moister cases differed by about 3% in power from the last rows. A gap that small lies within the uncertainty of the simulations.

Once cooling was allowed to respond, the same comparison produced a difference of 11%.

The cloud itself was responsible for the larger difference, according to the team’s analysis.

Heat is emitted upward by a cloud top, while water vapor in the overlying air radiates heat back down. Less heat is returned by drier air, so the top of the cloud cools more promptly.

Industry observers note that that stronger cooling stirred the air underneath more vigorously and the cloud-topped layer deepened. As a result, more of the wind’s energy was transported downward into the farm.

Energy arriving from above is most key at the back of a wind farm.

More than half of the power in the front rows comes from wind that flows in. Each row, however, leaves slower air in its wake for the rows that follow.

In the final rows of the simulated farm, turbulent mixing supplied up to about 90% of a row’s power.

It has been revealed that A second effect appeared when the air above the cloud was moister. The cloud-topped layer was then shallower and the approaching wind was slowed more strongly ahead of the farm. The first row of turbines produced less power as a consequence.

Temperature was also found to matter. In the runs with fixed cooling, the researchers varied the temperature contrast between the sea surface and the air above.

The air temperature was taken about 2 miles (3 kilometers) up. The farm’s output then differed by about 20% from a reference case.

Satellite images had already suggested that wind farms affect clouds.

On two mornings, June 5, 2016, and November 14, 2022, North Sea wind farms were photographed by NASA’s Terra satellite. The images highlighted partly cleared cloud near clusters of wind farms. The team took them from NASA Worldview.

In a recent development, the simulated thinning was strongest under two conditions. The base of the cloud was near the blade tips, and the cloud held little liquid water.

Sources indicate that in the run with the lowest cloud, the cloud layer’s top was 587 feet (179 meters) above the sea. That is below the blade tips.

Behind the farm, that cloud held up to 85% less liquid water than in a matching run without turbines.

Warmer, drier air from above was mixed into the cloud by turbulence from the turbines. More of the cloud’s water evaporated.

Ahead of the farm, the cloud changed the opposite way.

Recent findings suggest that the wind slowed as it approached the first row. In that same run, the cloud there held up to about 43% more liquid water than the incoming cloud.

The authors compared that to the Horns Rev wind farm. There, slowing wind ahead of the turbines has been linked to fog forming upwind.

According to recent reports, every run was set in the daytime, with the sun at a fixed angle. Sunlight weakens a low cloud, and the authors wrote that daytime conditions may have amplified the thinning.

The simulations also had no rain, a single farm layout, and the same large-scale wind in every run.

The simulated clouds thinned in the same general way as the photographed ones. The amounts were not compared.

Large clusters of wind farms weren’t simulated either. The authors wrote that those need more observations and more modeling.

Next, the team looks to simulate more kinds of weather and larger farms spaced farther apart. Selvatici noted that simulating real weather conditions will take more computing power than is available now.

The full study was published in the Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy.

#54178. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1559 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nomadicmatt ↗ Open Full Page

How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that drones are huge.
  • In a recent development, there’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1.
  • I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

In a recent development, there’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

Industry observers note that the sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Industry observers note that most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

In a recent development, the Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

Industry observers note that the drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most owners will likely never switch back.

Here’s a video of the drone in action:.

Recent findings suggest that the marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

In a recent development, while 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

Industry observers note that the Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that maryland Gov.
  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • It has been revealed that house Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

It has been revealed that house Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” remarked Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, mentioned he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a upcoming map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley stated he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

It has been revealed that democrats could also look to redraw the lines in Upcoming York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Upcoming York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

Industry observers note that it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the glitch. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where new maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Sources indicate that democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their newly introduced majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he noted.

#54176. Latest Update: Even powdery mildew can catch a fungal infection

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (949 w)

Latest Update: Even powdery mildew can catch a fungal infection

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers found a fungus that infects powdery mildew in preserved specimens, offering clues to how it might help control the crop disease.
  • Sources indicate that powdery mildew is usually the one doing the damage.
  • Researchers checked dried mildew specimens up to about 150 years old and found the parasite on mildews from many countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers found a fungus that infects powdery mildew in preserved specimens, offering clues to how it might help control the crop disease.

Sources indicate that powdery mildew is usually the one doing the damage. The fungi behind it infect crops such as wheat and grapevines, yet some of those mildews are infected themselves, by a fungus called Ampelomyces that lives inside their cells.

Researchers checked dried mildew specimens up to about 150 years old and found the parasite on mildews from many countries.

The study also found that about 13% of the public DNA records labeled Ampelomyces appear to belong to other fungi.

Michael Bradshaw, an assistant professor of entomology and plant pathology at North Carolina State University, led the research with first author Jacklyn Thomas.

Bradshaw directs the university’s Larry F. Grand Mycological Herbarium.

He sees the parasite as a possible tool against the disease. Part of the reason is host specificity, meaning some strains infect only certain kinds of mildew.

“By understanding hyperparasite diversity and how many different strains are out there, it might give us insights on if some are better at controlling the fungus than others,” Bradshaw said.

“There is a degree of host specificity to these hyperparasites, and if we are able to delve deeper they may be very useful in containing this plant disease.”.

According to recent reports, powdery mildews include more than 900 species. Together they cause disease in more than 10,000 kinds of flowering plants.

Powdery mildew fungi need living plant tissue to grow, so scientists can’t grow them in lab cultures. That makes their parasite hard to study as well.

So the team turned to herbaria, collections of preserved plants and fungi. The researchers screened 609 mildew specimens held at North Carolina State and at Harvard University’s Farlow Herbarium.

In a recent development, the specimens came from 28 countries, from Argentina and Morocco to Japan and Ukraine. Many reached North Carolina as gifts from herbaria in Germany and Japan.

From each specimen, the team scraped a bit of mildew and tested its DNA for the parasite.

The researchers then checked every positive result under a microscope.

Researchers lifted the mildew onto clear tape and found Ampelomyces under a microscope.

According to recent reports, ampelomyces turned up in 40 of the 609 specimens, or 6.6%. The authors wrote that old collections let them detect a parasite that is hard to observe directly.

Some kinds of mildew were infected far more often than others. Sawadaea mildews had the highest rate, at 14.3%.

Podosphaera and Phyllactinia mildews were among the lowest, at 3.2% and 2.7%.

Some of those groups had only a few specimens, the authors wrote, so small samples may explain part of the spread.

Researchers in Serbia and Hungary, examining field samples under a microscope, had found the parasite in about a third of them.

The detection rate in the herbarium specimens was much lower.

The authors suggested reasons for the gap. Their samples came from many parts of the world, and their DNA tests could miss strains whose genetic code differed from what the tests were built to match.

The team sorted its strains, along with hundreds from public records, by how closely related they were.

Strains from Podosphaera mildews tended to group together, and so did strains from a genus called Arthrocladiella.

Strains from Erysiphe, the largest mildew genus, were scattered across many groups.

The mix of tight groups and scattered strains suggests some Ampelomyces lineages specialize while others infect many kinds of mildew.

Several strains from the herbarium specimens matched no known group and may be latest lineages.

According to recent reports, one specimen of a mildew called Blumeria showed the parasite under the microscope, but its DNA test failed. The authors suggested that Ampelomyces on Blumeria may be a lineage not yet described.

Industry observers note that genBank is a public database where scientists share DNA sequences. The team downloaded all 671 sequences filed there as Ampelomyces and placed them in one family tree.

Of those sequences, 88 fell outside the main Ampelomyces branch. That is how the team arrived at its estimate that about 13% were probably other fungi.

Even samples from culture collections, which supply living strains to labs, were mislabeled.

One strain listed as Ampelomyces had DNA identical to a fungus called Didymella, though the authors wrote that it may have been contaminated after it left the collection.

Bradshaw noted errors like these are a risk whenever researchers rely on large datasets that anyone can add to.

“These parasites are hard to identify, so what happens is someone misidentifies them and enters incorrect data,” he said.

“Then someone else sees that wrong data and uses it to classify their own samples, which leads to more wrong data, and it amplifies that way.”.

The team’s answer is a checked reference tree of 47 confirmed strains, posted to a free online tool called T-BAS. Researchers can upload a sequence and see where it belongs.

According to recent reports, there are limits. The family tree rests mostly on one short piece of DNA, and its main Ampelomyces branch was only weakly supported.

More genetic data will help sort out how the strains are related, the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that two significant questions remain. Are some strains better at fighting the fungus than others?

And did the parasite and the mildew evolve together? Answering the second question will take more samples and whole genomes.

Future research could also expand sampling to more regions and more mildews.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings B.

Breaking: The fossil fuel ‘carbon bubble’ may be smaller than investors once feared

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced study estimates a $99.3 billion carbon bubble among major U.S.-listed fossil fuel companies, with climate policy risks varying by tech giant.
  • Major fossil-fuel companies may be overvalued by about $99.3 billion because of climate policy risks, according to new research.
  • That amounts to roughly 5.5% of the market value examined, suggesting investors have already priced in some of the transition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced study estimates a $99.3 billion carbon bubble among major U.S.-listed fossil fuel companies, with climate policy risks varying by tech giant.

Major fossil-fuel companies may be overvalued by about $99.3 billion because of climate policy risks, according to new research.

That amounts to roughly 5.5% of the market value examined, suggesting investors have already priced in some of the transition.

Researchers at the University of Technology Sydney’s Centre for Climate Risk and Resilience worked with colleagues at Macquarie University.

They investigated how major climate policy developments affected the value of leading fossil-fuel companies listed in the United States.

The findings suggest a smaller potential correction than some earlier estimates. They also point to considerable differences in how individual companies might fare.

The carbon bubble describes a concern about what fossil-fuel businesses are really worth as the world moves toward cleaner energy.

Industry observers note that their valuations depend partly on future earnings from coal, oil and gas. Stronger climate policies or falling demand could reduce those earnings, leaving reserves undeveloped and infrastructure less valuable.

According to recent reports, if investors underestimate those changes, share prices may be higher than future business prospects justify. A correction could then bring losses for shareholders and financial institutions.

The researchers set out to estimate that gap, while allowing for the possibility that markets already recognize some climate risks.

The team examined 31 major climate policy signals between 1996 and 2023.

These comprised 27 United Nations climate conferences and four significant announcements in the United States and European Union.

Using stock and options market information, they estimated firm values under two scenarios.

One assumed business as usual without additional climate-policy constraints; the other incorporated climate-related policy risks.

The difference produced the estimated bubble of 5.5%, or $99.3 billion, for the largest US-listed fossil-fuel companies with traded options.

According to recent reports, that figure concerns the companies studied. It does not measure the potential losses across every fossil-fuel business or project worldwide.

In a recent development, nor does it predict an inevitable crash. The results suggest markets may be adjusting gradually, with some transition risks already reflected in prices.

“The findings challenge the assumption that stronger climate policies must automatically lead to substantial financial losses for every fossil-fuel firm,” stated lead researchers Mona Mashhadi Rajabi and Martina Linnenluecke from Sydney.

Industry observers note that “Companies are not all equally exposed to the energy transition. Their financial position can depend on the quality of their assets, their investment decisions, their ability to adapt and how effectively they prepare for a changing energy market.”.

“This is an notable distinction. A company that recognizes transition risks early, adjusts its investment strategy and prepares for changes in energy demand may be better positioned than one that continues to rely on the assumption that current business conditions will last indefinitely.”.

The sector-wide estimate therefore leaves an key question for investors: which businesses are preparing, and which are counting on little changing?

A relatively modest estimate does not remove the uncertainty surrounding future fossil fuel demand.

Projects that look profitable today may earn less under different policies or more competitive clean-energy alternatives.

In a recent development, assets built to operate for decades are particularly exposed to those changes. Their economics depend on conditions well beyond the next reporting period.

“So, the key message of this research is not that fossil-fuel companies are financially safe. Significant transition risks remain, and these need to be assessed carefully. Importantly, risks will change as the stringency of carbon policies changes,” the scientists explained.

In a recent development, “For policymakers, the findings reinforce the importance of clear and predictable climate policies. For investors and financial institutions, the results are a reminder to look beyond headline estimates of stranded assets.”.

Stranded assets are reserves or infrastructure that lose economic value before their expected useful life ends. Their potential scale matters, but it cannot alone explain how a whole company will perform.

Industry observers note that investment choices, asset quality, and the ability to change direction also influence future earnings. Assessing those differences requires information about how companies intend to respond.

“Climate-related financial disclosure can help investors distinguish between companies that are preparing for the transition and those that remain heavily exposed to changing market conditions,” the researchers said.

According to recent reports, the research puts that distinction at the center of the debate. A single estimate of potential overvaluation cannot tell investors which projects will remain competitive or which strategies will work.

Recent findings suggest that for Australia, the findings have implications beyond the stock market. Decisions about new fossil-fuel projects commit money to assets whose working lives may span substantial changes in overseas demand.

“These questions are particularly vital for Australia, one of the world’s major exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas (LNG). The value of Australia’s fossil-fuel industries is closely connected to demand in international markets,” the authors wrote.

“Australia therefore needs to look beyond current export revenues when making decisions about future energy investment. A project that appears commercially attractive today may face a different economic outlook over its operating life.”.

“Equally, assuming that all fossil-fuel assets will rapidly lose value could lead to decisions that overlook differences in project economics and market exposure.”.

“The carbon bubble debate should move beyond predictions of a sudden collapse. What matters now is whether companies, investors and governments are making decisions that reflect the energy markets of the future, rather than relying solely on the conditions of the past.”.

The study is published in the journal Sustainable Futures.

#54173. Industry News: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1643 w)

Industry News: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • AI is already powering upcoming, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar.
  • Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

AI is already powering upcoming, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, notes AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”.

In a recent development, here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, indicates Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments indicated. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Sources indicate that still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.).

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan indicates. But fresh versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How promptly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

Recent findings suggest that the Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Sources indicate that guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

According to recent reports, the octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to blueprint how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler claims. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover newly introduced places to copy itself (third image).

Sources indicate that J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

Industry observers note that J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.).

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan notes they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers demonstrated another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan notes the organization’s work reveals that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

In a recent development, anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that revealed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

In a recent development, whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still major programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Sources indicate that guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”.

#54171. Tech Report: A vanished bird from Haiti may help solve an ancient Pacific mystery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1339 w)

Tech Report: A vanished bird from Haiti may help solve an ancient Pacific mystery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DNA reveals how snipes and woodcocks reached distant islands, stopped migrating, changed physically, and became vulnerable to extinction.
  • The sandpiper family includes some of the most extreme long-distance migrants among birds.
  • Recent findings suggest that two branches of that family, the snipes and the woodcocks, have behaved quite differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DNA reveals how snipes and woodcocks reached distant islands, stopped migrating, changed physically, and became vulnerable to extinction.

The sandpiper family includes some of the most extreme long-distance migrants among birds.

Recent findings suggest that two branches of that family, the snipes and the woodcocks, have behaved quite differently. These birds reached islands again and again, and migration was then abandoned.

Nearly every living species was examined in a latest DNA study.

The results suggest that island settlement was accompanied by changes in body size and flying ability. Island species later proved vulnerable when people arrived with rats and cats.

The work was led by Min Zhao, then a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. Colleagues at Virginia Tech and the Field Museum in Chicago also took part.

According to Zhao, the whole project grew out of one extinct bird from Hispaniola. That Caribbean island is shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

The dates reported in the study were estimated from family trees built with DNA. The uncertainty attached to them can run to millions of years.

Florida Museum researchers dug the bird’s bones out of a cave in Haiti in 1984.

In a recent development, in 2015, those bones were described by two scientists as a fresh species of woodcock. Woodcocks are long-billed birds that probe soft soil for food.

According to recent reports, one of the two scientists was David Steadman, who is now an emeritus curator at the museum. He is also listed as a co-author of the newly introduced study.

It has been revealed that zhao’s team extracted DNA from two of the fossil specimens. The researchers then read the mitochondrial genome, a small set of genes passed from mother to offspring.

It has been revealed that both specimens were placed with the snipes, which form the sister group of the woodcocks. Their closest living relative turned out to be the giant snipe of lowland South America.

The analysis suggested a South American origin for the Haitian bird’s ancestors. The two lineages are thought to have split between 5 and 12 million years ago.

Why, then, did the bones resemble those of a woodcock? The authors think the bird’s build may have been altered by island living, which could explain the mix-up.

Sources indicate that the outer wing bone of the Haitian bird was unusually short when compared with its upper wing bone. The authors wrote that it could fly but probably not well.

The team sequenced 45 samples in total. Two were the Haitian fossils and 19 were toe pads taken from old museum specimens. The remaining 24 were fresh tissue samples.

Recent findings suggest that all but one of the 29 living species of snipes and woodcocks were covered by these samples. Specimens were supplied by ten museums and research collections.

A family tree was built from the data, and both groups were traced back to Eurasia.

The ancestors of today’s American birds crossed from the Eastern Hemisphere to the Western Hemisphere four separate times.

One of those crossings took place roughly 20 million years ago. It was then that the ancestor of the American woodcock reached North America.

The researchers could not tell whether the bird arrived across the Atlantic or by way of Alaska.

The Austral snipes are found on the outlying islands of Upcoming Zealand. Scientists have long placed these small brown birds in a group of their own.

Some snipes from Eurasia spend each winter in Australia and on nearby islands. The DNA indicated that those visitors are not close relatives of the Austral snipes.

Instead, the Austral snipes share a branch with several large South American snipes and the extinct Haitian bird.

Two DNA datasets placed the split between the Austral snipes and their relatives at about 14 million and nearly 18 million years ago, respectively.

In a recent development, the southern continents had broken apart long before either estimate. The snipes’ ancestor most likely crossed the Pacific.

According to recent reports, how the crossing happened remains an open question. The authors suggested that birds straying far outside their normal range may have played a role. Such straying was perhaps caused by extreme weather.

The authors also raised a route through Antarctica. Patches of treeless tundra are thought to have lasted there until at least 12.8 million years ago.

Several living snipe species still breed on tundra in the Arctic.

The analysis indicated that the ancestors of both snipes and woodcocks were migrants. Their island descendants are not.

Ten of the 29 living species are found only on islands, and none of those ten migrates.

The habit was lost several times. Woodcocks gave it up when they settled the Malay Archipelago in Southeast Asia. Snipes did the same when they settled South America and Madagascar.

Body size changed as well, although not in a single direction.

The Amami woodcock of southern Japan is about 45% heavier than the Eurasian woodcock, its closest mainland relative. Madagascar’s snipe is about 91% heavier than the common snipe of Eurasia.

In a recent development, the opposite change is seen in the Austral snipes. Their average weight is 3.4 ounces (96 grams), which is about the weight of a deck of cards.

Recent findings suggest that south American snipes on the same branch average 8.6 ounces (243.5 grams). That is more than twice as much.

In a recent development, the smaller size may be explained by scarce food, the authors suggested. Competition from kiwis and other birds that probe the soil for worms was also considered possible.

Ten species of snipes and woodcocks are known to have died out in the recent geologic past. Nine of them lived on islands.

Industry observers note that the Austral snipes suffered the heaviest losses. Three of nine known species survive. All three are ranked as Vulnerable or Near Threatened by the IUCN Red List.

The South Island snipe died out in 1964, and introduced black rats are regarded as the likely cause.

No resident snipe or woodcock is left in the Caribbean. At least three species have been lost there.

According to recent reports, the youngest dated bones of the Haitian bird are about 600 years old. Rats and feral cats brought by people are suspected of causing its extinction.

Snipes nest on the ground, where they can be reached by those predators. Island species had given up migration, and in some cases strong flight as well.

The authors wrote that these changes made such species especially vulnerable to human impacts.

Overhunting was named as one of those impacts.

Jessica Oswald, a co-author, also worked on the study at the Florida Museum.

Sources indicate that “People will eat anything,” noted Oswald. She said a crew of hungry explorers or whalers could wipe out an island’s birds in a single weekend.

Island woodcocks in Japan and Southeast Asia appear to have fared better. They live in mountain forests, which may be harder for people to reach.

Latest Zealand may have been reached first by the Austral snipes.

According to recent reports, from there they could have spread to Norfolk Island, Latest Caledonia and Fiji. The opposite path cannot be ruled out, because no genetic data exist for those islands’ extinct snipes.

According to recent reports, more snipe species may once have lived in the Pacific and are now extinct. In that case, today’s birds would be the last survivors of a larger group. Direct fossil evidence of that link across the Pacific is still missing.

The Haitian bird’s place on the tree rests on mitochondrial genes from two specimens. A possible close relative from Puerto Rico is also extinct and has not been tested genetically.

The authors suggest that DNA from fossils yet to be found on Pacific islands could help trace how snipes spread across the region.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#54170. Could Earth have been collecting dark matter for billions of years?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (996 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Could Earth have been collecting dark matter for billions of years?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Heat measurements from dead stars helped physicists narrow down how dark matter might interact with ordinary matter.
  • Physicists have spent decades building dark matter detectors deep underground, and they still haven’t caught a single particle.
  • A newly introduced study suggests that Earth itself, along with the Sun, Jupiter and a handful of dead stars, might trap certain kinds of dark matter better than any lab instrument.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heat measurements from dead stars helped physicists narrow down how dark matter might interact with ordinary matter.

Physicists have spent decades building dark matter detectors deep underground, and they still haven’t caught a single particle.

A newly introduced study suggests that Earth itself, along with the Sun, Jupiter and a handful of dead stars, might trap certain kinds of dark matter better than any lab instrument.

These bodies could have been collecting slow-moving particles for billions of years.

The researchers used neutrino data and heat measurements to rule out some combinations of particle mass and interaction strength that laboratory experiments couldn’t probe.

The work was led by Alejandro Ibarra from the Technical University of Munich, Merlin Reichard from the Korea Institute for Advanced Study and Gaurav Tomar from the Sogang University in Seoul.

It has been revealed that about 85% of the matter in the universe is dark matter. We know it’s there because galaxies spin faster than their visible matter can explain and light bends more than it should as it passes them.

Industry observers note that beyond that, very little is known about it. Physicists are stuck in a frustrating loop.

You can’t identify something you can’t see, and you can’t design a way to see it without some idea of what it is. So they make a guess, build an experiment to test it, and so far the answer has always been no.

Recent findings suggest that one guess is that dark matter isn’t completely dark. Its particles might respond to electricity and magnetism very faintly, carrying a tiny fraction of an electron’s charge or acting like microscopic magnets.

The paper describes five such properties. One of them, the “anapole moment,” is a doughnut-shaped kind of magnetism.

Any of the five would let a dark matter particle occasionally bump into an atom.

It has been revealed that underground detectors wait for those bumps. A slow particle taps an atom so gently that the instrument doesn’t notice.

In practice, these detectors are more sensitive to faster dark matter particles.

Planets and stars work the other way around. A fast particle shoots straight through them. A slow one only needs to lose a little speed in a collision before gravity grabs it and won’t let go.

Over billions of years, trapped particles would sink toward the center and crowd together. Once packed tightly enough, they could meet and annihilate, turning into other particles.

In a recent development, some of those would be neutrinos, which pass through rock almost as if it weren’t there. The rest would deposit their energy as heat.

“In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” Tomar said.

“There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”.

For the Sun and Earth, the team used limits from IceCube, a detector built into the Antarctic ice, and from its smaller companion detector, DeepCore.

That included ten years of IceCube data on neutrinos coming from Earth’s core. There was no excess.

Neither Jupiter nor the white dwarfs generate heat through nuclear fusion.

The Cassini spacecraft measured how much heat Jupiter leaks from its interior.

Sources indicate that the white dwarfs are burnt-out stellar cores in M4, a cluster of ancient stars. Each one holds about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass in a ball with a radius of roughly 1,250 kilometers.

If a candidate type of dark matter would make these objects give off more heat than they actually do, it can be crossed off.

Earth turned out to be the best test for dark matter with a tiny electric charge. For particles heavier than about ten protons, it set the strongest limits yet.

There are two reasons. First, a charged particle’s pull reaches a long way, so it is easily drawn in. Second, Earth’s core is full of iron, whose atoms each carry 26 protons, which makes collisions more likely.

The white dwarfs set leading limits on two of the more exotic properties, the charge radius and the anapole moment, across a wide range of particle masses.

For very heavy particles, they also beat earlier limits on dark matter’s magnetic dipole moment.

The anapole limits matter for one popular candidate whose only possible electromagnetic property is the anapole moment.

For that candidate, the white dwarfs reach places that particle colliders and underground detectors struggle to get to.

Industry observers note that jupiter was a letdown. In general, it didn’t improve on limits that already existed. None of the four bodies beat earlier limits on the electric dipole moment either.

Underground labs sit beneath a kilometer or more of rock to block cosmic rays. If dark matter interacts strongly with ordinary matter, that same rock could slow it down or stop it before it reaches the detector.

The shield could be hiding the very particles the experiment is looking for.

Industry observers note that planets and stars don’t have this problem. The more strongly dark matter interacts, the better they catch it.

According to recent reports, there is one important caveat. The more dark matter surrounds a star, the more of it the star can capture, and nobody has measured how much dark matter M4 contains.

The team had to rely on estimates from models.

“We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar noted.

Tomar suggests two places to look next. One is even colder white dwarfs in regions with more dark matter, where any extra heat would be easier to detect.

The other is beyond the Solar System, where exoplanets could serve as dark matter traps too.

The study is published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

It has been revealed that speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

It has been revealed that he must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

According to recent reports, if the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In a recent development, in an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

Recent findings suggest that he predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Industry observers note that massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, noted on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Recent findings suggest that hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries stated. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

In a recent development, last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The Fresh Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith remarked, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

Industry observers note that "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie revealed in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure indicates Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution indicates, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.
